title: Quantum Channel Stein's Lemma With An Exponential Strong Converse
authors: Minbo Gao, Zhengfeng Ji, Chenghua Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27196v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish the quantum channel Stein lemma at every fixed type-I error tolerance in [MATH] and prove an exponential strong converse under arbitrary adaptive strategies. For any finite-dimensional channel pair, the optimal type-II exponent equals the regularized channel relative entropy and is attained by parallel strategies. When this divergence is finite, every strictly larger type-II rate forces the probability of accepting the null hypothesis to decay exponentially, uniformly over strategies and quantum memories. The proof rests on a uniform Stinespring approximation: tensor powers of the null dilation are approximated by tensor powers of the alternative dilation after applying an auxiliary linear map to the environment. The operator-norm error is exponentially small under a squared-norm bound at any rate above the regularized relative entropy. We construct the approximation from a weak testing bound by iterative rate reduction and a fixed-block tensor expansion with an exact residual. It implies right continuity at order one of the regularized sandwiched R\'enyi channel divergence, which yields the adaptive converse through the channel chain rule. We also obtain a sharp hockey-stick threshold and a subchannel smoothing asymptotic equipartition property for fixed and subexponentially vanishing diamond-norm errors.
tldr: The paper establishes the quantum channel Stein's lemma at every fixed type-I error and proves an exponential strong converse under arbitrary adaptive strategies.
motivation: Quantum hypothesis testing and channel discrimination are fundamental to quantum information theory, but a complete characterization of the Stein's lemma for quantum channels with strong converse under adaptive strategies was lacking.
method: The authors use a uniform Stinespring approximation to relate tensor powers of the null dilation to those of the alternative dilation via an auxiliary environment map, constructing the approximation from a weak testing bound, iterative rate reduction, and a fixed-block tensor expansion with exact residual.
result: For any finite-dimensional channel pair, the optimal type-II exponent equals the regularized channel relative entropy and is attained by parallel strategies; every strictly larger type-II rate forces exponential decay of the type-I error probability, uniformly over strategies and quantum memories.
conclusion: The work provides a tight characterization of quantum channel Stein's lemma with an exponential strong converse, implies right continuity of the regularized sandwiched Rényi channel divergence, and yields a sharp hockey-stick threshold and an AEP for subchannel smoothing with diamond-norm errors.

title: The Logical Set Of Gaussian States Under The Stabilizer Subsystem Decomposition
authors: Santiago Zamora, Kaustav Chatterjee, Ulrik Lund Andersen, Thiago Lucena de Macedo Guedes, Jonatan Bohr Brask, A. de Oliveira Junior, Rafael Chaves
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26898v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Universal quantum computation requires non-Gaussianity in continuous-variable systems and non-stabilizerness in discrete-variable systems. Yet, mapping a Gaussian state into the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill logical subspace can yield a logical qubit with non-stabilizer resources. To understand how the continuous-variable structure determines logical resources, we characterize the image of single-mode Gaussian states under the corresponding extraction channel, known as the stabilizer subsystem decomposition. Specifically, we derive series expressions for the logical Bloch vector and characterize the resulting reachable set, enabling an analytical treatment of the robustness of magic of the logical states. We then turn this geometric framework into a certification tool: by mapping a discrete-variable qubit witness to a continuous-variable squeezing witness, we obtain lower bounds on the squeezing of prepared states. We also show that ensembles of Gaussian states can violate both stabilizer and classical bounds. Violation of the stabilizer bound certifies the relational resource known as "set-magic," while violation of the classical bound enables the certification of cryptographic randomness at moderate squeezing.
tldr: The paper characterizes the logical states obtained from single-mode Gaussian states under the stabilizer subsystem decomposition, deriving the logical Bloch vector and reachable set to analyze non-stabilizerness and enable certification.
motivation: Understanding how continuous-variable Gaussian structure determines logical resources in Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill encodings is important for quantifying and certifying non-stabilizer magic in CV quantum information.
method: The authors derive series expressions for the logical Bloch vector and characterize the reachable set of single-mode Gaussian states under the extraction channel, turning the geometry into certification tools by mapping qubit witnesses to squeezing witnesses and analyzing Gaussian-state ensembles.
result: They obtain lower bounds on squeezing of prepared states, show that Gaussian-state ensembles can violate both stabilizer and classical bounds, and demonstrate certification of set-magic and cryptographic randomness at moderate squeezing.
conclusion: This work provides an analytical geometric framework connecting CV Gaussian states to logical non-stabilizerness, with practical applications for resource certification and randomness generation.

title: Deterministic Photon Waveform Adaptation For Quantum Connectivity
authors: Jeffrey Mohan, J\'er\'emy Berroir, Filippo Borselli, David Libault, Ferhat Loubar, Kilian M\"uller, Jed Rowland, F\'elix Hoffet, Eleni Diamanti, Tom Darras, Tommaso Mazzoni, Julien Laurat
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The scalability of quantum technologies will depend on the ability to interconnect independent quantum systems through photonic channels. However, heterogeneous quantum platforms emit and absorb photons with widely differing properties, severely limiting inter-node interference and modular connectivity. Here we demonstrate a cold-atom optical quantum memory that simultaneously achieves near-unity storage-and-retrieval efficiency and deterministic temporal adaptation of single photons between arbitrary and programmable input and output pulse waveforms. Operating at high optical depth and within a fully integrated architecture, the system can store photons with durations spanning over three orders of magnitude and reshape them arbitrarily without compromising efficiency, achieving compatibility with many current platforms. By augmenting the role of a quantum memory from a passive storage element to an active programmable photonic interface, our results establish a key building block for scalable entanglement-based quantum networks and modular quantum computing architectures.
tldr: A cold-atom optical quantum memory achieving near-unity efficiency and deterministic, programmable temporal reshaping of single photons as an active photonic interface for quantum connectivity.
motivation: Scalable quantum technologies require interconnecting heterogeneous quantum platforms, but their emitted photons differ in duration and waveform, severely limiting inter-node interference and modular connectivity.
method: A high-optical-depth, fully integrated cold-atom quantum memory stores single photons whose durations span three orders of magnitude and deterministically reshapes them between arbitrary, programmable input and output pulse waveforms.
result: Near-unity storage-and-retrieval efficiency is maintained while photons are temporally adapted between arbitrary waveforms, yielding compatibility with many current quantum platforms.
conclusion: Elevating a quantum memory from passive storage to an active programmable photonic interface provides a key building block for scalable entanglement-based quantum networks and modular quantum computing.

title: Transparent Domain Walls Through Information Convex Sets
authors: Jintae Kim, Amanda Gatto Lamas, Jacopo Gliozzi, Bowen Shi, Taylor L. Hughes, Jong Yeon Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In [MATH]-dimensional topologically ordered many-body states, transparent (topologically deformable) domain walls are invisible to local topological probes, yet can modify the ground state degeneracy (GSD) and transmute anyons transported across them. Here, we develop an entanglement-bootstrap framework using information convex sets (ICSs) on local and noncontractible annuli to extract information about transparent domain walls directly from ground state wavefunctions at fixed points of Abelian topological phases on a torus, without taking categorical defect data as input. We derive fusion rules governing the action of anyons on extreme points of ICSs on noncontractible annuli and determine their quantum dimensions. Extreme points invariant under transport around the complementary cycle correspond one-to-one to minimum entropy states (MESs), and their number equals the GSD. The maximal topological entanglement entropy (TEE), [MATH], probes the net effect of walls crossing the chosen annulus, where [MATH] is the total quantum dimension and [MATH] is the quantum dimension of an extreme point of its ICS. In contrast, the maximal entanglement asymmetry is [MATH]. This value is the same for both annulus orientations and reflects the combined effect of the transparent domain walls. We further show that transparent domain walls can give rise to symmetries supported jointly on the two chosen fundamental cycles that cannot be decomposed into a product of two [MATH]-form symmetry operators, one supported on each cycle. By relating their action on MESs to anyon tunneling and the fusion rules, we clarify how these symmetries connect distinct ground states. Additionally, we apply the framework to Wen's plaquette model, the anisotropic dipolar toric code, and the rank-2 toric code.

They derive fusion rules for anyons acting on extreme points of ICSs on noncontractible annuli and determine their quantum dimensions. A key result is that extreme points invariant under transport around the complementary cycle correspond one-to-one with minimum entropy states (MESs), and their number equals the ground-state degeneracy (GSD). The maximal topological entanglement entropy (TEE) is given by γ_LW^max = log(D/d_α), where D is the total quantum dimension and d_α is the quantum dimension of an extreme point, probing the net effect of walls crossing the annulus. The maximal entanglement asymmetry is ΔS_X^max = log GSD, independent of annulus orientation, reflecting the combined effect of transparent domain walls. title: Soft Decoding For Quantum Ldpc Codes With Experimental Validation
authors: Arda Aydin, Edwin Tham, Nicolas Delfosse, Min Ye
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The decoder is a critical component of a fault-tolerant quantum computer, computing corrections based on parity-check measurements performed throughout the computation. A soft decoder supplements its output with a confidence score which, when used alongside post-selection, can substantially improve logical performance. We introduce a soft beam search decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes that uses internal decoder data as a confidence metric, removing the need for extra computation. We perform circuit-level simulations of five quantum LDPC codes relevant for superconducting and trapped ion architectures equipped with our global soft decoder and we obtain up to [MATH] logical-error suppression at a physical error rate of [MATH] while rejecting only [MATH] of shots. Then, we simulate an error detected measurement, which is a core logical operation of the walking cat architecture, using a streaming version of soft beam decoder and we achieve up to [MATH] error suppression while increasing the rejection probability by only [MATH] percentage points. Finally, we revisit recent quantum LDPC code memory experiments on trapped ions, demonstrating that our soft decoder doubles the logical qubit lifetimes at the price of a mean rejection rate of [MATH]--[MATH] per syndrome round, bringing all five codes into the beyond-breakeven regime.
tldr: Introduces a soft beam search decoder for quantum LDPC codes that uses internal decoder data as a confidence metric, achieving significant logical error suppression and beyond-breakeven performance in simulations and trapped-ion experiments.
motivation: Decoders are critical for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and soft decoding with post-selection can substantially improve logical performance, but often requires extra computation.
method: The authors develop a soft beam search decoder for quantum LDPC codes that extracts confidence scores from internal decoder data, removing additional computation, and simulate five relevant codes plus a streaming version for error-detected measurement in the walking cat architecture.

conclusion: Soft decoding can practicaly enhance quantum LDPC code performance with low rejection overhead, validating its use for fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.

The decoder is designed for fault-tolerant quantum computing, where decoders process parity-check measurements to compute corrections. By providing a soft output (confidence score), the decoder allows rejection of unreliable shots, significantly improving logical performance. The authors perform circuit-level simulations of five quantum LDPC codes relevant to superconducting and trapped-ion architectures, demonstrating up to 580× logical-error suppression at a physical error rate of 10^-3 while rejecting only 0.1% of shots. They also simulate an error-detected measurement, a core operation in the walking cat architecture, using a streaming version of the soft beam decoder, achieving up to 210× error suppression with only a 0.5 percentage point increase in rejection probability. Finally, they revisit recent quantum LDPC code memory experiments on trapped ions, showing that their soft decoder doubles logical qubit lifetimes at the cost of a mean rejection rate of 2.6%–5.6% per syndrome round, bringing all five codes into the beyond-breakeven regime.

This soft output is then used in post-selection: shots with low confidence are rejected. The authors perform circuit-level simulations, which include realistic noise models for superconducting and trapped-ion architectures, to evaluate the performance of five quantum LDPC codes. title: Efficient Learning Of Clifford-Scrambled Product States
authors: Tobias Haug
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27128v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clifford circuits acting on product magic states provide a compact ansatz exhibiting extensive magic, volume-law entanglement, and even classically hard sampling under standard complexity assumptions. Here, we efficiently recover its hidden product subsystems from two-copy Bell sampling. Quadratic relations between Bell samples determine the irreducible blocks after removing Pauli stabilizers, and binary linear algebra constructs a Clifford disentangler. For logarithmic-size blocks, approximate learning of the full state is efficient whenever the state remains inverse-polynomially separated from acquiring additional Pauli stabilizers. We efficiently learn [MATH]-qubit states prepared by random [MATH]-doped Clifford circuits with [MATH]-gate density below one via [MATH] Bell samples, and disentangle hidden product blocks in Clifford-augmented matrix product states. For unitary learning, we exactly learn [MATH]-depth-one circuits using [MATH] queries. Finally, we rule out pseudorandom states and unitaries with a product bipartition hidden by Clifford circuits.

title: Sample-Efficient Tomography Of A Class Of Mixed States With Extensive Entanglement And Magic
authors: Quntao Zhuang Pengcheng Liao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27177v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Full tomography of a generic many-qubit quantum state requires exponentially many copies, while suitable structural constraints can make reconstruction sample-efficient. Existing approaches exploit, for example, limited entanglement structure, low magic, or constrained state-preparation circuits. Here we consider a class of mixed states that can simultaneously exhibit extensive entanglement and extensive magic. Specifically, we introduce Clifford-encoded block-product (CEBP) states, obtained by applying an unknown global Clifford unitary to a tensor product of arbitrary mixed states supported on unknown blocks of bounded size. We show that, for a fixed block size, CEBP states can be reconstructed using polynomially many copies by exploiting Clifford-preserved Pauli correlations to recover the latent structure and reduce the remaining problem to local tomography. Our result demonstrates that sample-efficient tomography can arise from bounded complexity in a latent frame even when the physical state is highly entangled, highly magical, and mixed, and suggests complexity modulo structured transformations as a broader organizing principle for quantum-state learnability.

conclusion: The work suggests complexity modulo structured transformations as a broader organizing principle for quantum-state learnability.

title: Limits For Molecular Spectroscopy From Quantum Channel Discrimination
authors: Anirban Dey, Akib Karim, Pieter Kok, Mark M. Wilde, Zixin Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Absorption spectroscopy identifies molecules by detecting frequency-dependent optical loss, and its fundamental limit is a quantum channel-discrimination problem. In this work, we develop a general framework for characterizing the ultimate quantum limit of molecular absorption spectroscopy without collective measurements: we formulate it as an asymmetric quantum hypothesis testing task between different absorption channels. Using a semidefinite-programming formulation, we construct optimal probe states and compare them with coherent-state photon counting, Fock states, and two-mode squeezed vacuum probes. We introduce a random-loss channel model for imperfectly known background transmission, reflecting the fact that a blank experiment need not return all incident photons due to scattering, solvent absorption, or collection losses. Our results show that optimized non-classical probes can substantially outperform conventional laser spectroscopy, and that the advantage is robust to realistic baseline random loss. % In multi-frequency spectroscopy, the optimization also determines how photons should be allocated across absorption lines, revealing an additional resource-allocation advantage beyond single-mode state engineering. We illustrate our framework using infrared detection of 4-nitrophenol against chemically relevant comparison molecules, showing how quantum channel-discrimination methods provide constructive performance limits for molecular spectroscopy under realistic photon constraints.
tldr: Formulates molecular absorption spectroscopy as asymmetric quantum channel discrimination and computes ultimate limits and optimal probe states via semidefinite programming.
motivation: Absorption spectroscopy's fundamental limit can be viewed as a quantum channel-discrimination problem, but practical constraints and imperfect background transmission require a general framework without collective measurements.
method: Models different molecular absorption channels and uses semidefinite programming to find optimal probe states, comparing coherent-state photon counting, Fock states, and two-mode squeezed vacuum probes under a random-loss background channel.
result: Optimized non-classical probes outperform conventional laser spectroscopy, and this advantage remains robust under realistic baseline random loss; multi-frequency spectroscopy also reveals an additional photon-allocation advantage.
conclusion: Quantum channel-discrimination methods provide constructive performance limits for molecular spectroscopy under realistic photon constraints, illustrated by infrared detection of 4-nitrophenol against chemically relevant comparison molecules.

title: Higher-order Spatially Separated Correlations And Quantum Magic In The Long-range Transverse Field Ising Model

title: Antiblockade Quantum Batteries
authors: Yao Yao Guohui Dong
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Blockade, a phenomenon in which one particle hinders the transport of another, constitutes a core research topic in mesoscopic and microscopic physics. Benefiting from the unique single-particle characteristics, it underpins versatile applications spanning from quantum computation to quantum metrology. Nevertheless, in the context of quantum energy?storage devices, i.e., quantum batteries (QBs), blockade triggered by the intrinsic level splitting is in turn detrimental to energy accumulation. Here we propose an antiblockade charging protocol enabled by deliberately engineering a bright-dark interaction. Rooted in a manifold of equally-spaced dressed-dark states, this elaborate configuration opens up a new charging channel facilitating an antiblockade energy flow and outperforms the Rabi-split blockade design with at least a 20-fold enhancement in energy storage. Additionally, we further illustrate the achievement of superextensive (quadratic) charging characteristic by operating the system in the bad-cavity limit. In view of its inherent generality, our scheme offers a universal and feasible pathway toward high-performance quantum energy architectures.

result: The antiblockade protocol achieves at least a 20-fold enhancement in energy storage over the Rabi-split blockade design and can exhibit superextensive (quadratic) charging in the bad-cavity limit.
conclusion: The scheme offers a universal and feasible pathway toward high-performance quantum energy architectures by exploiting antiblockade effects.

title: Influence Of Fast And Slow Laser Phase Noise On The Fidelity Of The M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen Trapped-ion Gate
authors: Nikita Semenin, Ksenia Khabarova, Nikolay Kolachevsky
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-fidelity two-qubit entangling gates are essential for the realization of useful quantum algorithms on quantum processors. The M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen (MS) gate has become a common choice for trapped-ion quantum computing due to its resilience to ion temperature and its demonstrated record fidelities. However, the spectral impurity of the driving laser field impacts gate performance, with phase noise influencing the qubit dynamics through mechanisms operating on different timescales. In this work, we present a comprehensive theoretical analysis of laser phase noise in the MS gate, identifying two spectral ranges which influence the gate fidelity the most: "fast" noise at frequencies near the motional mode spectrum, and "slow" noise at frequencies on the order of the inverse gate time. We derive the noise Hamiltonians for two common laser beam geometries and obtain analytical expressions for the average gate error in terms of the laser noise power spectral density and gate parameters. title: Monolithic Quantum Error Correction In The Presence Of Distinguishability
authors: Shubham P. Jain, Eric R. Hudson, Wesley C. Campbell, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Victor V. Albert
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum error-correcting codes require that the environment cannot distinguish relevant error processes acting on different codewords. In practice, residual Zeeman, Stark, or anharmonic interactions shift the underlying states, making errors distinguishable and weakening the conditions for perfect recovery. We study this effect with an analytically solvable four-level model and a canonical spontaneous-emission noise model for atoms and molecules. Distinguishability raises the effective Kraus rank of the noise channel, lowers the recovered fidelity, and sets an operational checking time that shortens as the frequency separation between the emitted photons increases. We find that rapid syndrome checking suppresses the buildup of distinguishability and quantify how fast one needs to check to restore near-perfect recovery. Error distinguishability is thus a practical limitation of monolithic error correction, and our analysis identifies fast syndrome extraction as a route to mitigating it.

title: Coherence-Enhanced Spatial Quantum Thermometry
authors: Asghar Ullah, Giovanni Scala, Luis L. S\'anchez-Soto, \"ozg\"ur E. M\"ustecapl{\i}o\u{g}lu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum thermometry has long promised sensitivities beyond classical limits, with recent paradigms highlighting quantum coherence as a primary driver of precision. Adding auxiliary TLSs shifts the array's optimal working temperature upward and broadens the useful sensing window, with the achievable gain ultimately limited by the total available coupling rather than by an indefinite scaling law. Finally, we propose a microwave Mach-Zehnder interferometer that maps the temperature-dependent probe coherence onto an experimentally accessible quadrature observable.

title: Precision And Resource Scaling Of Real-time Flux Distortion Compensation For Superconducting Quantum Control
authors: Qi Zhou, Zi-Hao Mei, Peng Duan, Peng Wang, Liang-Liang Guo, Hao-Ran Tao, Wei-Cheng Kong, Hui Yang, Guo-Ping Guo, Zhao-Yun Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-time waveform generation supports dynamic quantum circuits without pre-storing complete waveforms for every execution path. title: Measurement-Only Dynamical Phase Transitions In Spin-1 Chains
authors: Kemal Aziz, Haining Pan, J. H. Pixley
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study measurement-only dynamics in an interacting spin-1 chain, using forced, normalized local projections rather than Born-rule-sampled measurement outcomes. Starting from the nearest-neighbor (NN) Affleck-Kennedy-Lieb-Tasaki (AKLT) Haldane symmetry-protected topological state, we show that competing local projectors drive this order toward three distinct dynamical phases: a featureless topologically trivial product state, an explicitly dimerized valence-bond-solid state, and a topologically trivial next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) AKLT state consisting of two interwoven Haldane chains. Using matrix product state and exact statevector simulations, we identify continuous transitions among these phases and characterize them using nonlocal string order parameters, local dimer order, and entanglement scaling. For the NN-NNN AKLT model, finite-size signatures are consistent with an intervening extended critical regime rather than a single direct transition. These results extend studies of monitored topology to a bosonic SPT and show that local projections can control both topological and valence-bond-solid order.
tldr: Measurement-only dynamics in a spin-1 chain, driven by competing local projectors, reveals three distinct dynamical phases and continuous transitions characterized by entanglement scaling and string order parameters.
motivation: To extend studies of monitored topology to bosonic symmetry-protected topological (SPT) states and understand how local projections can control both topological and valence-bond-solid order.
method: Matrix product state and exact statevector simulations of forced, normalized local projections applied to the nearest-neighbor AKLT state, with analysis via nonlocal string order parameters, dimer order, and entanglement scaling.
result: Three dynamical phases emerge: a trivial product state, a dimerized valence-bond-solid state, and a next-nearest-neighbor AKLT state, with continuous transitions and evidence for an extended critical regime in the NN-NNN AKLT model.
conclusion: Local projections can deterministically drive and control topological and valence-bond-solid order in spin-1 chains, highlighting measurement-only protocols as a tool for engineering quantum phases.

title: Measurement-based Feedback As A Flexible Tool To Control non-Poissonian Photon Statistics
authors: Ming Li, Junyan Luo, Georg Engelhardt
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Poissonian photon statistics are usually traced to nonlinear interactions, nonclassical states, or engineered reservoirs. Here we show that measurement-based feedback can be alternatively deployed to control the Poissonian character of the measurement statistics in an externally-driven linear cavity. Each photon detection triggers a weak displacement operation whose phase determines how the feedback interferes with the coherent cavity field, resulting in a significant cavity response. Full counting statistics and two-time photon correlations show that the feedback phase controls the sign and strength of the induced correlations, continuously tuning the emission statistics between super- and sub-Poissonian regimes. At generic phases, the Mandel parameter responds linearly to the feedback amplitude, whereas at specific phases, the leading response becomes quadratic. The same phase dependence is also found in higher-order cumulants of the emission statistics. These results establish measurement-based feedback as a route to controlling photon statistics in otherwise linear driven-dissipative systems.
tldr: Measurement-based feedback on a driven linear cavity can tune photon emission statistics between super- and sub-Poissonian regimes via the feedback phase.
motivation: Non-Poissonian photon statistics are typically attributed to nonlinear interactions, nonclassical states, or engineered reservoirs, and this work asks whether measurement-based feedback can alternatively control them in a linear system.
method: Each photon detection triggers a weak displacement operation whose phase controls interference with the coherent cavity field; the authors compute full counting statistics and two-time photon correlations.
result: The feedback phase controls the sign and strength of induced correlations, continuously tuning the Mandel parameter between super- and sub-Poissonian regimes, with linear response at generic phases and quadratic response at special phases, mirrored in higher-order cumulants.
conclusion: Measurement-based feedback provides a flexible tool to control photon statistics in otherwise linear driven-dissipative systems.

By tuning this feedback phase, the authors demonstrate continuous control over the emission statistics, transitioning between super-Poissonian and sub-Poissonian regimes. The analysis employs full counting statistics and two-time photon correlation functions to characterize the induced correlations. The Mandel parameter is shown to respond linearly to the feedback amplitude at generic phases, but quadratically at specific phases. Higher-order cumulants exhibit the same phase dependence. The work establishes measurement-based feedback as a versatile tool for engineering photon statistics in otherwise linear systems, without requiring nonlinearities or nonclassical resources.

title: Sustained Growth Of Quantum Circuit Complexity In Many-body Hamiltonian Dynamics
authors: Wonjun Lee, Sa\'ul Pilatowsky-Cameo, Soonwon Choi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26885v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quantum circuit complexity of an evolving many-body quantum system is believed to exhibit a sustained growth, maintained for timescales much longer than the onset of thermalization. Most previous works have focused on models which violate energy conservation, such as random unitary circuits. Here we study generic, local time-independent Hamiltonian dynamics. We unconditionally prove that for generic local Hamiltonians and typical initial product states at high effective temperature, the robust quantum circuit complexity must grow over a very long period of time, attaining an exponentially large value at late times. Our approach relies on two structural properties that we prove rigorously: (i) generic local Hamiltonians satisfy generalized spectral no-resonance conditions of arbitrary order, and (ii) typical high-temperature product states are effectively supported in exponentially many energy eigenstates. These properties have been widely assumed without proof in prior works. As corollaries of this result, we show the late-time state displays robust volume-law entanglement that is irremovable by polynomial-size circuits, and we establish a no fast-forwarding result for generic local Hamiltonians. We also lower bound the complexity of preparing sufficiently large subsystems with local quantum channels, in contrast with sufficiently small thermalizing regions which we show retain low complexity at late times.
tldr: They prove that generic local time-independent Hamiltonians exhibit sustained growth of robust quantum circuit complexity from typical high-temperature product states, reaching exponentially large values at late times.
motivation: Quantum circuit complexity is believed to grow long after thermalization, but most previous works focus on energy-nonconserving random unitary circuits rather than generic local Hamiltonian dynamics.
method: They rigorously prove generalized spectral no-resonance conditions for generic local Hamiltonians and show that typical high-temperature product states are supported on exponentially many energy eigenstates.
result: Complexity grows over a very long period and becomes exponentially large; late-time states have robust volume-law entanglement irremovable by polynomial-size circuits, and no fast-forwarding is possible.
conclusion: This establishes complexity growth in generic many-body Hamiltonian systems, validates previously assumed structural properties, and provides bounds on subsystem preparation complexity.

title: Quantum Soundness Of A Total-Degree Line-versus-Point Test
authors: Tianrun Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27129v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove quantum soundness of the total-degree diagonal line-vs-point test using the individual-degree soundness theorem of Ji, Natarajan, Vidick, Wright, and Yuen. A random change of coordinates yields projective polynomial decoders of total degree at most [MATH]. The uniform-line slice of the test bounds the weight of outcomes of degree greater than [MATH], which are removed by a common relabeling. This reduction does not yield a dimension-independent soundness bound: the [MATH] dependence of the individual-degree theorem persists, as discussed in Section 1.2 of arXiv:2009.12982.
tldr: The paper proves quantum soundness for the total-degree diagonal line-versus-point test by reducing it to the individual-degree soundness theorem.
motivation: Low-degree tests are central to probabilistically checkable proofs and quantum complexity, but the total-degree line-versus-point test lacked a quantum soundness proof.
method: A random change of coordinates constructs projective polynomial decoders of bounded total degree, while uniform-line slicing and common relabeling remove high-degree outcomes.
result: Quantum soundness is established, but the reduction inherits the dimension dependence of the individual-degree theorem and does not yield a dimension-independent soundness bound.
conclusion: The work advances the quantum soundness analysis of low-degree tests, though a dimension-independent bound remains open.

title: Dual Boundary Condition Inference: A Two-Boundary Product Rule And Its Implications
authors: Eliahu Cohen Luis Razo
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27120v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many inference problems are constrained from two sides: forward information and a second constraint on outcomes. Dual Boundary Condition Inference (DBCI) multiplies them and renormalises. The rule is not new: it is the product-of-experts form and the unit-exponent member of the logarithmic-pooling family. The paper contributes a classification and reducibility characterisation. The algebra does not fix the exponent at which the inputs combine: given the statistic log p_fwd + log p_bwd, which already builds in the product form, maximum entropy supplies the family (p_fwd p_bwd)^lambda and selects no member. If the inputs are read as two equally weighted opinions, three requirements select lambda = 1/2: unanimity preservation, consistency under a common Bayesian update, and minimal symmetric Kullback-Leibler divergence. If they are read as separately applied factors, two requirements select lambda = 1: a neutral second input must leave the first unchanged, and an update to one input must pass through unchanged. For a rank-one intermediate projective measurement, the Aharonov-Bergmann-Lebowitz (ABL) rule realises this form with no extra parameter. Every positive exponent orders outcomes identically, so the choice is invisible to picking the likeliest outcome, but not to scoring a class by total mass. Under the relevant identifications, the same product form gives Bayes' rule, while a final effect proportional to the identity returns the ordinary forward Born probabilities. The second result is a Two-Boundary Reducibility Criterion: DBCI factors through the forward boundary exactly when the effective backward boundary, up to positive rescaling, does. So a fixed prior or model-fixed structural constraint adds no distinctions between cases sharing the same forward boundary, though it may encode substantial information and still materially affect the result.
tldr: The paper classifies dual boundary condition inference as a logarithmic pooling rule and derives exponent-selection criteria, linking it to the ABL rule and Born probabilities.
motivation: Many inference problems combine forward information with a second constraint, but the algebra of the product rule does not by itself fix the exponent at which the two inputs combine.
method: The authors use maximum entropy, Bayesian consistency, KL divergence, and quantum measurement examples to characterize when the exponent is 1/2 versus 1, and they prove a two-boundary reducibility criterion.
result: Three requirements select lambda=1/2 for equally weighted opinions, two requirements select lambda=1 for separately applied factors, and the ABL rule realizes lambda=1; all positive exponents order outcomes identically, though they differ in total class mass.
conclusion: The product rule is not new, but the paper provides a classification and reducibility characterization; prior or model-fixed structural constraints add no distinctions between cases sharing the same forward boundary even if they encode information.

title: Finite-Sample Binary Hypothesis Testing Via R\'enyi Divergences: Strong Converse And Local Privacy
authors: Roberto Bruno, Adrien Vandenbroucque, Amedeo Roberto Esposito
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study asymmetric simple binary hypothesis testing between [MATH] and [MATH], based on [MATH] independent and identically distributed observations. Leveraging a variational representation of R\'enyi divergence of order [MATH], we derive our main result: a finite-sample converse with [MATH]. The bound uses both directions of the divergence [MATH] and [MATH], tensorises under product measures, and contains familiar data-processing converses as boundary cases. For comparison, we apply the same variational approach to general [MATH]-divergences and specialise it to total variation, [MATH], Hellinger, and Kullback Leibler divergences, thereby recovering familiar converses within a unified framework. Together with an achievability bound involving R\'enyi divergence with [MATH], the main converse recovers the phase transition of the optimal Type II error under the exponentially decaying Type I error constraint [MATH]. Under regularity conditions, the optimal Type II error vanishes exponentially when [MATH]. We also derive sample-complexity bounds and extend both the converse and achievability analyses to locally differentially private observations, quantifying the cost of privacy and recovering the non-private achievability bound as the privacy constraint vanishes.
tldr: The paper derives finite-sample converse bounds for binary hypothesis testing using Rényi divergences and extends the analysis to locally differentially private observations.
motivation: To provide a unified framework for finite-sample hypothesis testing bounds via variational representations of Rényi divergences, including privacy constraints.
method: Leverages a variational representation of Rényi divergence to derive a finite-sample converse involving both directions of the divergence, tensorises under product measures, and applies to general f-divergences.
result: The converse recovers the phase transition of the optimal Type II error, provides sample-complexity bounds, and quantifies the cost of local differential privacy.
conclusion: The unified approach recovers familiar converses and extends to locally private settings, showing the privacy cost vanishes in the non-private limit.

title: Programmable Coherent Memory Kernels For Quantum Reservoir Computing In Waveguide Qed
authors: Hong Jiang, Yu Wu, Yue Ban, Xi Chen, Juan Jos\'e Garc\'ia-Ripoll
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reservoir computing requires not only long memory, but also memory distributed over the timescales relevant to a given task. In most quantum reservoir computing architectures, however, the memory profile emerges from intrinsic dynamics and cannot be directly engineered. Here we introduce a waveguide-QED quantum reservoir in which coherent memory return is controlled by the coupling geometry. The reservoir consists of a driven Kerr-nonlinear resonator coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide at spatially separated points. An unmeasured propagating field carries information about past inputs and coherently returns it to the resonator after a finite propagation time, forming a non-Markovian feedback channel without intermediate measurement or classical reinjection. Delay-resolved memory benchmarks reveal two complementary functions: waveguide propagation determines when past information returns, whereas Kerr dynamics convert the returned field into nonlinear temporal features accessible through a linear readout. NARMA-[MATH] prediction shows that the optimal feedback delay shifts systematically with task order and approximately tracks the explicit input-product lag. These results establish coherent delayed feedback as a mechanism for engineering task-relevant memory in quantum reservoir computing.
tldr: A waveguide-QED quantum reservoir uses coherent delayed feedback from a Kerr-nonlinear resonator to engineer programmable memory kernels for quantum reservoir computing.
motivation: Quantum reservoir computing typically relies on intrinsic dynamics, giving limited control over the memory timescales needed for temporal tasks.
method: The authors model a driven Kerr-nonlinear resonator coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide at separated points, creating an unmeasured non-Markovian feedback channel, and benchmark it with delay-resolved memory tasks and NARMA prediction.
result: The waveguide propagation delay determines when past information returns, while Kerr dynamics generate nonlinear temporal features; the optimal feedback delay shifts with task order and approximately tracks the input-product lag.
conclusion: Coherent delayed feedback provides a mechanism to engineer task-relevant memory in quantum reservoirs, potentially improving temporal information processing in waveguide-QED architectures.

title: Equivalence Of Maximal And Generic Reachability For Non-universal Variational Quantum Circuits
authors: Michael Spannowsky Vishal S. Ngairangbam
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27053v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Employing problem-specific non-universal Variational Quantum Circuits aligned with a suitable state preparation has become a standard approach to counter the difficulty in training universal ans\"atze. However, due to their non-universality, diagnosing their reachability and trainability remains reference-state-specific. In this work, we establish the equivalence of maximal reachability and generic reachability over arbitrary reference states as a consequence of the . Thereafter, assuming that the global minimum of the cost function is achieved on a subset that can be described as the image of a smooth function, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for non-zero probability of reachability under generically sampled reference states. Furthermore, when the solution set is assumed to be realised through a real analytic map that embeds a solution manifold, we show that local surjectivity is generically obtained on the entire solution manifold if it is attained at a single point. As a practical design rule, the need for local surjectivity automatically translates to a necessary dimensional criterion: reachability requires the target set's topological dimension to be at least as large as the co-dimension of the generic orbit. Numerical simulations show that finite-depth optimisation consistently fails when the dimensional obstruction applies, while unobstructed cases show improved convergence.
tldr: The paper studies reachability and trainability of non-universal variational quantum circuits, establishing equivalence between maximal and generic reachability and deriving a topological dimension criterion for obstruction.
motivation: Problem-specific non-universal variational circuits are widely used but their reachability is reference-state-dependent, making diagnosis and design difficult.
method: The authors use geometric and topological arguments, including smooth maps, real analytic maps, and topological dimension, supported by numerical simulations of finite-depth optimization.
result: They prove equivalence of maximal and generic reachability, give necessary and sufficient conditions for non-zero reachability probability, and show that local surjectivity on a solution manifold follows from attainment at a single point; simulations confirm failures when the dimensional obstruction applies.
conclusion: The work provides a practical dimensional design rule for non-universal variational quantum circuits and clarifies when finite-depth optimization can succeed.

title: Uphill And Downhill First Passage Of An Active Brownian Particle: Asymmetry And Exact Path Reweighting
authors: Mykola Tasinkevych, Xuan My Le, Artem Ryabov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27425v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: First passage processes in active systems combine stochastic transport with self-propulsion and orientational persistence, making motion along and against an external bias sensitive to the internal active dynamics. For passive biased diffusion, opposite exits can have different splitting probabilities while their conditional first passage time distributions remain identical. We study how this relation changes for an active Brownian particle driven by a constant external force between two absorbing boundaries. Self-propulsion breaks the equality of the uphill and downhill first passage time distributions and modifies the splitting probabilities. Nevertheless, the two directional path ensembles remain exactly related by spatial reflection, which pairs downhill and uphill first passage paths of the same duration while preserving their orientational history. The log-ratio of the probabilities of a path and its reflected partner defines a path-dependent asymmetry functional and provides an exact reweighting between the two ensembles. In the symmetric half-weighted representation, the uphill and downhill first passage time distributions coincide for arbitrary orientational persistence. The same path relation also allows rare uphill statistics to be reconstructed from the more frequently sampled downhill trajectories. Numerical simulations confirm the weighted equality across the explored bias and persistence regimes, while perturbative and asymptotic analyses clarify how orientational persistence produces the directional asymmetry of the unweighted statistics. The exact relation between the two directional path ensembles suggests that similar symmetry-based reconstruction protocols may be found in other nonequilibrium first-passage problems.
tldr: The paper studies uphill versus downhill first-passage statistics of an active Brownian particle and shows the two directional path ensembles are exactly related by spatial reflection, yielding an exact reweighting scheme.
motivation: Passive biased diffusion has identical conditional uphill/downhill first-passage time distributions despite different splitting probabilities, and the authors ask how self-propulsion and orientational persistence break this symmetry.
method: Exact path-integral/path-probability analysis of an active Brownian particle between two absorbing boundaries under constant bias, combined with a reflection-based path reweighting functional, perturbative expansions, asymptotics, and numerical simulations.
result: Self-propulsion breaks the equality of uphill and downhill first-passage distributions, but the two path ensembles remain exactly related by spatial reflection; the log-ratio of reflected path probabilities defines a path-dependent asymmetry functional that exactly reweights one ensemble into the other, and in the half-weighted representation the two distributions coincide for arbitrary persistence.
conclusion: The exact reflection relation permits reconstructing rare uphill statistics from more frequent downhill trajectories and suggests symmetry-based reconstruction protocols for other nonequilibrium first-passage problems.

title: Optimising Cryogenic Wiring For Microwave-frequency Millikelvin Quantum Processors
authors: Adrien Di Lonardo, Giorge Gemisis, Juan Pablo Dehollain, Nathan K. Langford
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27239v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cryogenic capacity is a key bottleneck in the scaling of superconducting quantum processors, critically impacted by control wiring. Currently, wiring architectures are often designed following a small set of "best-practice" heuristics, little changed since they emerged for early, small-scale systems, and not rigorously evaluated for wider contexts. Here, we adopt a whole-system numerical modelling approach and present a systematic optimisation for the coaxial wiring design of a superconducting quantum processor. We identify optimised configurations that substantively outperform conventional designs in device temperature, noise burden, qubit capacity and other practical metrics. Importantly, our analysis delivers varied outcomes for different system contexts and operating regimes, illustrating the benefits of a systematic approach when there is no universal solution. Our results evaluate and sometimes challenge conventional wisdom in relation to design factors such as the utility of 0dB attenuators. We also use a wide exploration of cable configurations---directly enabled by our holistic and flexible numerical modelling approach---to develop more rigorously supported general principles for future cryogenic system design, based on a new conceptual framework to describe attenuator cascades that draws on analogies to low-noise amplifier chains. Our approach, design outcomes, and generalised analyses should also be readily applicable to other cryogenic quantum computing platforms. Finally, we support ready adoption of this approach through a web-based graphical tool which streamlines the analysis of the proposed framework under different contexts. Our results illustrate how our approach can help maximise the available computational resources of quantum processors at all system scales.
tldr: The paper numerically optimizes cryogenic coaxial wiring for millikelvin superconducting quantum processors, showing that conventional design heuristics are not universally optimal across operating regimes.
motivation: Cryogenic capacity and control wiring are key bottlenecks for scaling superconducting quantum processors, yet wiring architectures still rely on little-evaluated best-practice heuristics.
method: Whole-system numerical modeling systematically explores coaxial wiring and attenuator-cascade configurations, supported by a web-based graphical tool for different system contexts.
result: Optimized configurations outperform conventional designs in device temperature, noise burden, and qubit capacity, and challenge practices such as the blanket utility of 0 dB attenuators, with no universal optimum.
conclusion: The proposed attenuator-cascade framework and systematic optimization can improve cryogenic system design and help maximize available computational resources across quantum computing platforms.

title: The Sharp R\'enyi And Tsallis Threshold In The Shepp--Olkin Concavity Problem
authors: Haoran Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27433v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be independent Bernoulli random variables with parameters [MATH], and let [MATH]. Hillion and Johnson proved that the Shannon entropy of [MATH] is jointly concave in the parameter vector and proposed corresponding critical-order conjectures for R'enyi and Tsallis entropies, with predicted thresholds [MATH] and approximately [MATH], respectively. We determine both thresholds exactly. For every [MATH], the power sum [MATH] is jointly concave in [MATH], and strictly concave on the open parameter cube. Consequently, the R'enyi and Tsallis entropies of order [MATH] are jointly concave. At [MATH] this agrees with the Shannon theorem. For every [MATH], joint concavity fails already for the sum of two Bernoulli variables: a transverse interpolation in which the two parameters move in opposite directions gives strict local convexity for both entropies. Hence the universal joint-concavity range for both families is exactly [MATH].
tldr: This paper exactly determines the critical orders for joint concavity of Rényi and Tsallis entropies of sums of independent Bernoulli random variables, resolving conjectured thresholds in the Shepp-Olkin concavity problem.
motivation: Hillion and Johnson proved Shannon entropy is jointly concave and conjectured specific critical-order thresholds for Rényi and Tsallis entropies, but these thresholds were not known exactly.
method: The author analyzes the joint concavity of power sums of the Bernoulli parameter vector and uses transverse interpolation to construct local convexity counterexamples above the threshold.
result: For every order up to a critical value, the power sum and hence the Rényi and Tsallis entropies are jointly concave, with strict concavity on the open cube; for larger orders, concavity fails already for two Bernoulli variables.
conclusion: The universal joint-concavity range for both Rényi and Tsallis entropies is determined exactly, confirming and sharpening the conjectured thresholds and recovering the Shannon case as a special point.

title: A Non-Invasive Cloud-Based Migration Strategy For Post-Quantum Cybersecurity In Smart Hvac Systems: Architecture, Implementation, And Empirical Evaluation
authors: Mahedee Zaman Moon, Kaysarul Anas Apurba, Md Hasibul Hasan, Sk Md Mizanur Rahman
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27828v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Legacy smart HVAC controllers rely on vendor-cloud TLS secured by ECDH and RSA, both broken by Shor's algorithm, and typical 10-15 year lifespans mean today's devices remain in service through the quantum-threat era. Direct on-device post-quantum cryptography is infeasible: an ESP32-S3, representative of capable HVAC hardware, has only 339 KB free heap against the 900 KB ML-KEM-768 requires, and even classical ECDH-P256 keygen (111.93 ms) dwarfs hardware AES-128 (0.032 ms). We propose a non-invasive PQC proxy, requiring no device, firmware, or vendor-cloud changes, performing ML-KEM-768 encapsulation and ML-DSA-65 authentication (NIST FIPS 203/204) with AES-256-GCM session keys via HKDF, implemented with Open Quantum Safe liboqs on a Raspberry Pi 4B gateway. Over 500 runs, the post-quantum handshake (Steps 1-6) completes in 2.48 ms, 0.38 ms slower than classical baseline, with PQC computation around 8% of handshake time at 20 ms simulated round-trip network latency. The gateway sustains 443 sessions/second, 100% success under 32 concurrent connections, extrapolating to 3546 sessions/second on a 32-core cloud instance. Five side-channel tests, including verified in-place session-key zeroization and a fixed-vs-random TVLA timing analysis, found no exploitable timing leakage or susceptibility to man-in-the-middle attacks. The architecture is vendor-agnostic and becomes unnecessary once vendors adopt NIST PQC natively.
tldr: The paper proposes a non-invasive cloud-based post-quantum cryptography proxy to secure legacy smart HVAC controllers against quantum attacks without modifying devices or vendor clouds.
motivation: Legacy smart HVAC systems rely on RSA/ECDH TLS that Shor's algorithm can break, and direct on-device PQC is infeasible due to severe memory and computational constraints on microcontrollers like ESP32-S3.
method: A Raspberry Pi 4B gateway running Open Quantum Safe liboqs performs ML-KEM-768 encapsulation, ML-DSA-65 authentication, and AES-256-GCM session keys via HKDF, acting as a transparent proxy.
result: The post-quantum handshake completes in 2.48 ms (0.38 ms slower than classical), sustains 443 sessions/second with 100% success, and passes five side-channel tests including TVLA timing analysis.
conclusion: The architecture is vendor-agnostic and provides a practical migration path for legacy systems until vendors adopt NIST PQC natively.

title: Free-fermion Spectral Structure Enables Strange Nonchaotic Attractor Classification In Aubry-Andre-Harper Quantum Reservoirs
authors: Suresh Kumarasamy, Dianavinnarasi Joseph, Manish Dev Shrimali, Awadhesh Prasad
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An Aubry-Andr\'{e}-Harper (AAH) quantum reservoir classifies strange nonchaotic attractors (SNAs) against chaos, substantially outperforming reservoirs built from dense random matrices on the full Fock space. Ablations and controlled interventions identify , rather than proximity to a quantum phase transition, as the dominant factor under our controls, since [MATH] is quadratic in fermion operators and only [MATH] of the [MATH] Fock-space transitions carry weight. Random on-site disorder, which preserves this quadratic structure, matches AAH accuracy, whereas full-Hilbert-space random matrices and eigenvector permutations, which break it, collapse to the random baseline. We characterize the resulting frequency-selective filtering with a Hamiltonian transition kernel, validate it to [MATH] qubits, and reproduce it in a second dynamical system. We also use the reservoir as a training-free screen for strange-nonchaotic structure in Kepler RR Lyrae light curves.
tldr: An Aubry-André-Harper quantum reservoir classifies strange nonchaotic attractors against chaos, with free-fermion spectral structure—not proximity to a quantum phase transition—as the key enabling factor.
motivation: Strange nonchaotic attractors (SNAs) are challenging to distinguish from chaos, and it is unclear what properties of quantum reservoirs govern their classification performance.
method: The authors use an AAH quantum reservoir, perform ablations with random on-site disorder, full-Hilbert-space random matrices, and eigenvector permutations, characterize the resulting filtering via a Hamiltonian transition kernel, validate on up to several qubits, and test on Kepler RR Lyrae light curves.
result: The quadratic free-fermion structure of the AAH Hamiltonian is identified as dominant; random disorder preserving this structure matches AAH accuracy, while breaking it collapses performance to the random baseline, and the effect is reproducible in a second dynamical system.
conclusion: Free-fermion spectral structure enables frequency-selective filtering that can serve as a training-free screen for strange-nonchaotic structure in time-series data.

abstract: ArXiv:2609.26858v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report on a Penning trap based on NdFeB permanent magnets operated at 4\,K with a magnetic field strength of 280\,mT. Reliable loading and confinement of protons, H[MATH] ions, and electrons was demonstrated with non-destructive single-particle detection sensitivity of protons and H[MATH] ions using superconducting image-current circuits. The axial frequency of individual particles reaches a shot-to-shot stability of 47 parts-per-billion comparable to that of state-of-the-art precision Penning-trap experiments. Measurements of the proton modified-cyclotron frequency show a shot-to-shot scatter of [MATH] parts per million (p.p.m.), presently limited by millikelvin-level temperature fluctuations of the permanent-magnet assembly. We outline a route towards improving this performance by more than an order of magnitude. This development offers broad potential for axial-mode-related precision measurements and cost-efficient Penning-trap experiments, and represents an important step towards compact, scalable, and transportable antiproton-trap systems.
tldr: A compact Penning trap built from NdFeB permanent magnets and operated at 4 K achieves single-particle detection of protons, H2+ ions, and electrons with axial frequency stability of 47 ppb.
motivation: Conventional Penning traps rely on large, power-hungry superconducting solenoid magnets, which limits portability and increases cost; the authors aim to show that permanent-magnet traps can reach useful precision for fundamental measurements.
method: A permanent-magnet Penning trap with a 280 mT field was cryogenically operated at 4 K, with non-destructive single-particle detection via superconducting image-current circuits; axial and modified-cyclotron frequencies of individual trapped particles were measured.
result: Protons, H2+ ions, and electrons were reliably loaded and confined, with axial frequency shot-to-shot stability of 47 ppb and modified-cyclotron frequency scatter of a few ppm, currently limited by millikelvin-level temperature fluctuations of the magnet assembly.
conclusion: The device demonstrates a route toward compact, scalable, transportable antiproton and precision Penning-trap experiments, with a proposed performance improvement of more than an order of magnitude.

title: Structured Variational Key Concentration For A Reduced Aes Cipher
authors: Xi Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26800v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Grover search provides the generic quantum baseline for symmetric-key recovery by amplifying a reversible public-verification oracle. We investigate whether public round structure can instead shape a variational key register before exact verification. For simplified AES (S-AES), we construct phase separators from S-box differential-distribution constraints, candidate-key-dependent inverse diagnostics, and a global residual Hamming-shell term. Each component has a reversible compute-phase-uncompute realization. We prove a one-sided completeness statement for these diagnostics and derive a conditional lower-tail bound for false keys under a weakly correlated diagnostic model. On ten random three-pair 16-bit S-AES instances, an 18-layer schedule optimized with Adam achieves a mean public-consistent-key probability of 46.78 percent, ranks the correct key first in every run, and limits the largest observed false-key probability to 1.11 percent. The 16-bit study evaluates the induced key-register dynamics without shot sampling, while a separate gate-level S-DES experiment validates the reversible oracle pattern without a key-space phase table. The results establish a controlled reduced-cipher benchmark; they do not claim an attack on full AES or an asymptotic advantage over Grover. Within these limits, the construction provides a useful framework for analyzing how AES structure can be incorporated into quantum algorithms.
tldr: A variational quantum algorithm that uses public round structure of S-AES (phase separators from S-box differential constraints, inverse diagnostics, Hamming-shell terms) to concentrate probability on the correct key, benchmarked on 16-bit reduced ciphers.
motivation: Grover search is the generic quantum baseline for symmetric-key recovery, but it ignores public round structure; the authors ask whether such structure can be folded into a variational key register to improve key concentration before exact verification.
method: Construct reversible compute-phase-uncompute diagnostics from S-box differential-distribution constraints, candidate-key-dependent inverse checks, and a global residual Hamming-shell term, optimized by an 18-layer Adam-trained variational schedule, with a separate gate-level S-DES experiment validating the oracle pattern.
result: Across ten random three-pair 16-bit S-AES instances, the schedule reaches a mean public-consistent-key probability of 46.78%, ranks the correct key first in every run, and keeps the largest false-key probability at 1.11%; a one-sided completeness proof and a conditional lower-tail bound on false keys are provided.
conclusion: The work is a controlled reduced-cipher benchmark showing how AES structure can be incorporated into quantum algorithms, without claiming an attack on full AES or an asymptotic advantage over Grover.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Sampling Of Schr\"odinger Bridges
authors: Eyal Neuman Tom Lollier
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the dynamic Schr\"odinger bridge problem on a finite state space and exploit its Markov structure to decompose the problem into an endpoint coupling and a collection of conditional Markov bridges. To sample from the conditional bridges, we develop a quantum Gibbs sampler based on quantum walks on the bridge path space. Under uniformly positive transition probabilities, we derive a spectral-gap bound and provide an explicit procedure for preparing the initial state. Compared with the update bounds of the corresponding classical Gibbs sampler, our quantum walk-query complexity improves the dependence on the time horizon [MATH] from quadratic to linear. For the endpoint coupling, we adapt a quantum box-constrained Newton method to compute the Schr\"odinger potentials, improving the matrix-scaling complexity, at fixed accuracy, from quadratic to [MATH] in the state-space size [MATH]. Finally, we show that exponential reweighting extends both the Schr\"odinger bridge formulation and the Gibbs spectral-gap estimate to models with additive running costs.
tldr: Quantum algorithms for sampling Schrödinger bridges using quantum walks and a quantum Newton method achieve improved complexity in time horizon and state-space size.
motivation: The dynamic Schrödinger bridge problem is computationally challenging, and classical samplers have unfavorable scaling with time horizon and state-space size.
method: The problem is decomposed into an endpoint coupling and conditional Markov bridges; a quantum Gibbs sampler based on quantum walks samples the bridges, and a quantum box-constrained Newton method computes the Schrödinger potentials.
result: Under uniformly positive transition probabilities, the quantum walk-query complexity improves the time-horizon dependence from quadratic to linear, and the matrix-scaling complexity for the endpoint coupling improves from quadratic to sub-quadratic in the state-space size.
conclusion: Quantum enhancements provide provable speedups for Schrödinger bridge sampling, and exponential reweighting extends the approach to models with additive running costs.

title: A 75-mL Intrinsically Stable Atom-filtered Laser Enabling Deployable Quantum Devices
authors: Zijie Liu, Zheng Xiao, Zhiyang Wang, Xiaolei Guan, Xiaomin Qin, Suyang Wei, Hongtian Song, Baoshuai Wang, Jia Zhang, Xiaopeng Xie, Tiantian Shi, Anhong Dang, Jingbiao Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27447v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Numerous quantum devices require lasers strictly locked to atomic transitions. Atom-filtered lasers (AFLs) are considered a leading candidate for quantum device laser sources due to their ability to self-align to atomic transitions. However, the sub-GHz sharp transmission spectra of conventional atomic filters impose constraints on both laser miniaturization and output stability. Herein, we demonstrate a micro Faraday anomalous dispersion optical filter ({\mu}FADOF) operating within the extreme hyperfine Paschen-Back regime, generating a 7.5 GHz flat-top transmission window. By integrating this filter, the miniaturization bottleneck of the AFLs is overcome, achieving a 30-fold volume reduction to a compact package volume of 75 mL. Simultaneously, investigations into the optical self-feedback characteristics of the {\mu}FADOF reveal a stable operating regime, where the optical self-feedback of the atomic filter acts as a stabilizing mechanism, enabling the laser to achieve a power instability of 9 x 10^-6 at 1 s and 3.2 x 10^-5 at 8400 s. The optical frequency standard based on this 75-mL AFL achieves a further improvement in long-term frequency stability to 3 x 10^-13 at 10000 s and maintains turn-key operation under environmental shocks, highlighting the critical role of this laser in the development of deployable quantum devices.
tldr: Demonstrated a 75 mL intrinsically stable atom-filtered laser using a micro Faraday anomalous dispersion optical filter for deployable quantum devices.
motivation: Many quantum devices require lasers strictly locked to atomic transitions, but conventional atomic filters suffer from sub-GHz sharp transmission spectra that limit both miniaturization and output stability.
method: Integrated a micro Faraday anomalous dispersion optical filter operating in the extreme hyperfine Paschen-Back regime to generate a 7.5 GHz flat-top transmission window and explored optical self-feedback for stabilization.
result: Achieved a 30-fold volume reduction to 75 mL, power instability of 9e-6 at 1 s, and long-term frequency stability of 3e-13 at 10000 s with turn-key operation under environmental shocks.
conclusion: The compact, stable atom-filtered laser overcomes miniaturization bottlenecks and could enable deployable quantum devices and portable optical frequency standards.

title: First Passage In The Presence Of Jump Rate Fluctuations: A Transition From Infinite To Finite Mean
authors: Shlomi Reuveni Bara Levit
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A simple symmetric random walk on a one-dimensional lattice is guaranteed to reach any target site, yet its mean first-passage time diverges. Here, we show that stochastic fluctuations in the jump rate can fundamentally alter this classic result. We find a phase transition in the mean first-passage time: sufficiently broad rate fluctuations render it finite, whereas weaker fluctuations leave it infinite. Our results demonstrate that temporal fluctuations in the jump rate---and hence in the diffusivity---can overcome spatial wandering and regularize otherwise divergent first-passage times.
tldr: The paper shows that stochastic fluctuations in the jump rate of a classical random walk can induce a phase transition that makes the mean first-passage time finite instead of divergent.
motivation: Classical random walks on a one-dimensional lattice always reach a target but have divergent mean first-passage time; the authors ask whether temporal fluctuations in the jump rate can regularize this divergence.
method: They analyze a simple symmetric random walk with a stochastically fluctuating jump rate and derive conditions on the fluctuation strength for finite versus infinite mean first-passage time.
result: Sufficiently broad rate fluctuations render the mean first-passage time finite, while weaker fluctuations leave it infinite, demonstrating a phase transition in this quantity.
conclusion: Temporal fluctuations in diffusivity can overcome spatial wandering and regularize otherwise divergent first-passage times, revealing a novel mechanism in classical stochastic transport.

title: Asymptotic Quasi--local Structure Induced By Magnetic Field
authors: Giuseppe de Nittis
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a magnetic coherent--state frame over the Landau levels of the two--dimensional Landau Hamiltonian, indexed by a discrete metric space combining spatial and energy degrees of freedom. Although overcomplete, the frame is almost--orthogonal, and we use it to endow the CAR [MATH]--algebra over the one--particle Hilbert space with an (AQL) structure, in which graded commutators of observables localized on disjoint index sets decay exponentially rather than vanish exactly. By means of a family of conditional expectations onto the resulting local subalgebras, we construct a Fr\'echet [MATH]--subalgebra of almost--local observables, invariant under the discrete group of lattice translations, which act on it by continuous automorphisms. For the full continuous group of magnetic translations we establish a quantitative control on how local observables spread through this almost--local algebra, and we show that this control suffices to extend graded asymptotic abelianness from the lattice to the entire continuous translation group. The results provide a discrete--continuum dictionary intended as the starting point for extending Lieb--Robinson--type techniques from lattice systems to interacting continuum electrons in a magnetic field.
tldr: Introduces a magnetic coherent-state frame on Landau levels to define an almost-quasi-local (AQL) structure for CAR algebras, enabling Lieb-Robinson-type analysis for continuum electrons in a magnetic field.
motivation: To extend Lieb-Robinson bounds and locality techniques from lattice systems to interacting continuum electrons in magnetic fields, which requires a discrete-continuum dictionary.
method: Constructs a discrete metric space from spatial and energy degrees of freedom, defines conditional expectations onto local subalgebras, and analyzes the spread of observables under magnetic translations.
result: Shows exponential decay of graded commutators for disjoint index sets and extends graded asymptotic abelianness from the lattice to the full continuous translation group with quantitative control.
conclusion: Provides a framework for applying Lieb-Robinson-type techniques to continuum magnetic systems, bridging lattice and continuum locality.

title: High-power Visible Laser Via Injection Locking To A Photonic Integrated Circuit Optical Parametric Oscillator
authors: Daniel Pimbi, Zhiquan Yuan, Ashish Chanana, Usman A. Javid, Xiyuan Lu, Jordan Stone, Kartik Srinivasan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27215v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kerr photonic integrated circuit optical parametric oscillators (PIC OPOs) provide a promising platform for coherent visible-light generation, offering broad wavelength accessibility and low frequency noise for applications in quantum information processing, precision metrology, spectroscopy, and sensing. However, achieving large fiber-coupled output powers and high conversion efficiency remains challenging, impacting the practical deployment of these sources. Here we demonstrate optical injection locking of a commercially available visible Fabry-P\'erot (FP) laser diode to a PIC OPO, realizing a hybrid laser that combines the complementary strengths of nonlinear frequency conversion with those of semiconductor laser technologies. Using 25 [MATH]W of injected PIC OPO signal, we generate coherent visible-light at 635 nm with a fiber-coupled output power of [MATH] 40 mW and side-mode suppression ratio [MATH] 36.3 dB. The injection-locked FP laser faithfully inherits the low frequency noise characteristics of the PIC OPO signal, achieving a frequency noise floor of 714 Hz[MATH]/Hz. We further demonstrate [MATH] GHz wide locking bandwidths that enable stable injection locking without active PIC OPO stabilization, together with coarse wavelength tunability over 6 nm while preserving both high output power and spectral purity. Our results establish optical injection locking with nonlinear light sources as a compelling option for coherent, high-power, and wavelength-agile integrated coherent visible sources.
tags: photonic integrated circuit optical parametric oscillator
tldr: Injection locking a commercial Fabry-Perot laser diode to a photonic integrated circuit optical parametric oscillator yields a high-power, low-noise, tunable visible coherent source at 635 nm.
motivation: PIC OPOs offer broad wavelength accessibility and low frequency noise for quantum information processing and metrology, but achieving high fiber-coupled output power and conversion efficiency remains challenging.
method: The authors optically injection-lock a visible Fabry-Perot laser diode to a PIC OPO signal, measuring output power, side-mode suppression ratio, frequency noise, locking bandwidth, and coarse wavelength tunability.
result: They obtain 40 mW fiber-coupled output power at 635 nm, a side-mode suppression ratio of 36.3 dB, a frequency noise floor of 714 Hz/√Hz, GHz-wide locking bandwidth, and 6 nm coarse tunability while preserving high power and spectral purity.
conclusion: Optical injection locking with nonlinear light sources is a compelling approach for coherent, high-power, wavelength-agile integrated visible sources.
keywords: photonic integrated circuit optical parametric oscillator

title: Minimal Representations Of Topology-preserving Quantum-like States
authors: William Horvat, Debadrita Saha, Nicol\'as Gigena, Prineha Narang, Gregory D. Scholes
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27318v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We provide an equitable partition that gives an exact, minimal representation for the graph Cartesian product formed from quantum-like bits that preserves the relevant spectral and topological properties. We show that this result follows from the fact that the operations of taking the Cartesian product of graphs and constructing equitable partition of the graphs commute. Numerical simulations illustrate the preserved emergent eigenstates in the reduced structures. Additionally, we provide a construction of the minimal structure without passing through the Cartesian product. Finally, we frame quantum-like structures in the language of topology and fibrations.
tldr: The paper constructs minimal equitable-partition representations of graph Cartesian products that model quantum-like bits, preserving spectral and topological properties.
motivation: To provide an exact reduction of complex graph-based quantum-like structures while retaining emergent eigenstates and topological features.
method: It proves that taking the Cartesian product of graphs commutes with constructing equitable partitions, and gives a direct construction of the minimal structure without the Cartesian product, framed via topology and fibrations.
result: An exact minimal representation is obtained, and numerical simulations illustrate the preservation of eigenstates in the reduced structures.
conclusion: This offers a graph-theoretic framework for topology-preserving reduction of quantum-like states, with potential relevance to graph-based quantum models but no direct connection to the four prioritized research directions.

title: Observable Lyapunov Exponents For Globally Coupled Maps In The Mean-Field Limit
authors: Matteo Tanzi Masood Ahmad
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27484v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large coupled systems may be chaotic at the microscopic level while exhibiting stable collective behaviour at the macroscopic level. Distinguishing between these two forms of instability has been a problem in the physics literature, and several approaches have been proposed.
