A deconvolution procedure then suppresses noise and extracts the third-order response from the total signal. The analysis enables correction of spectral intensities and unambiguous assignment of spectral features to the molecular response. This work pushes multidimensional spectroscopy toward the impulsive limit and enables integration with other nonlinear spectroscopies such as attosecond spectroscopy - all without compromising few-cycle pulse properties.
tldr: The paper develops an in-operando interferometric autocorrelation method to characterize and deconvolve pump spectral features from few-cycle coherent multidimensional spectroscopy signals.
motivation: Near single-cycle pulses greatly broaden the accessible spectral range and time resolution in coherent multidimensional spectroscopy, but self-phase-modulation-induced pump spectral structure contaminates the signal and complicates extraction of the molecular response.
method: An interferometric integrated autocorrelation measurement is run concurrently with the 2D spectroscopy experiment to retrieve the pump spectrum with matching time and frequency properties, followed by a deconvolution procedure that suppresses noise and isolates the third-order response.
result: The approach corrects spectral intensities and enables unambiguous assignment of spectral features to the molecular response, pushing multidimensional spectroscopy toward the impulsive limit.
conclusion: The technique allows integration with other nonlinear spectroscopies such as attosecond spectroscopy without compromising few-cycle pulse properties.

title: Gaussian-process Surrogate Indicators For Residual-based Adaptive GMsFEM
authors: Siqing Liu, Eric Chung, Yiran Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26843v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Residual-based adaptive GMsFEM for high-contrast elliptic problems repeatedly evaluates local weighted [MATH] indicators on every coarse neighborhood, making indicator evaluation a recurring cost in repeated-query settings. We introduce a non-intrusive Gaussian-process (GP) surrogate for the indicator scores used in D\"orfler marking. The operational predictor is the GP posterior mean, algebraically equivalent to a kernel ridge regression (KRR) estimator under the stated convention; it uses compressed local solution and spectral features without changing the multiscale solve, local spectral construction, or basis enrichment. A nonuniform perturbed-marking result quantifies how pointwise score errors affect the exact indicator mass captured by surrogate-selected neighborhoods, while a conditional bounded-discrepancy KRR pathway identifies sufficient assumptions for such score bounds. In controlled held-out in-distribution tests, the surrogate-guided method gives error-versus-DoF trends comparable with classical [MATH]-residual offline adaptivity and evaluates the online indicator component 2.0-2.1 times faster, excluding offline data generation and GP training.
tldr: The paper introduces a Gaussian-process (equivalently kernel ridge regression) surrogate for the local weighted residual indicators used in Dörfler marking within residual-based adaptive GMsFEM for high-contrast elliptic problems, achieving a modest online speedup.
motivation: Indicator evaluation on every coarse neighborhood is a recurring computational bottleneck in residual-based adaptive GMsFEM, especially in repeated-query or many-solve settings where adaptivity must be run many times.
method: A non-intrusive GP posterior-mean (KRR) surrogate predicts indicator scores from compressed local solution and spectral features, leaving the multiscale solve, local spectral construction, and basis enrichment unchanged; theory shows how pointwise score errors perturb the exact indicator mass captured by surrogate-selected neighborhoods.
result: In held-out in-distribution tests, the surrogate-guided adaptive scheme yields error-versus-DoF trends comparable to classical residual offline adaptivity while evaluating the online indicator component 2.0-2.1 times faster (excluding offline data generation and GP training).
conclusion: GP/KRR surrogates can cheaply approximate marking indicators in adaptive multiscale FEM, but the contribution is a numerical-analysis and scientific-computing advance with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum platforms.

title: Reconstruction And Range Characterization For A Directional Confocal Non-Line-of-Sight Imaging Model
authors: Lingyun Qiu, Zuoqiang Shi, Jianyu Wang, Shiwei Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the reconstruction of a directional albedo field from confocal non-line-of-sight measurements. For mirror-symmetric vector fields in Sobolev spaces, radial preprocessing reduces the data to spherical means of the divergence with centers on the relay wall. Full data determine this divergence uniquely, with divergence-free fields forming the entire ambiguity. An explicit Fourier--sine formula recovers the irrotational Helmholtz component and reproduces the data. The Fourier--sine transforms of the model data form a weighted Hilbert space that we characterize exactly, with norm equal to the Sobolev norm of the reconstructed field. This weighted range remains well defined even when the preprocessed data fail to belong to standard Sobolev spaces. For Schwartz fields in the model class, such Sobolev regularity holds exactly when the divergence has zero depth integral. Measurements on an open subset of the relay wall, for all radii [MATH], uniquely determine the divergence in the union of the corresponding balls. An FFT-based algorithm with Stolt interpolation implements the reconstruction in [MATH] operations on an [MATH] grid. Tests on explicitly defined fields assess reconstruction accuracy and invariance under divergence-free perturbations. We present imaging examples of potential and vector-field reconstruction from model-generated, rendered, and measured transients.
tldr: This paper develops reconstruction and range characterization for a directional confocal non-line-of-sight imaging model using spherical means and Fourier-sine methods.
motivation: The work aims to recover directional albedo fields from confocal non-line-of-sight measurements and to characterize the achievable data range in a mathematically rigorous way.
method: Radial preprocessing reduces the measurements to spherical means of the divergence, an explicit Fourier-sine formula recovers the irrotational Helmholtz component, and an FFT-based algorithm with Stolt interpolation implements the reconstruction.
result: Full data uniquely determine the divergence up to divergence-free fields, open-subset measurements determine the divergence in the union of corresponding balls, the weighted Fourier-sine range equals the Sobolev norm of the reconstructed field, and the algorithm runs in O(N^2 log N) on an N×N grid.
conclusion: The paper provides a mathematical framework and efficient algorithm for directional confocal non-line-of-sight imaging, validated on synthetic, rendered, and measured transients.

title: Reflectionless Measures With Singular Continuous Components On Widom Sets
authors: Long Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27133v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a detailed implementation of the mass-splitting construction of Nazarov, Volberg and Yuditskii for reflectionless measures with singular continuous components. The finite approximants are allowed to have isolated atoms. An exact local operation replaces each active atom by a short permanent interval and two child atoms, thereby eliminating the dependence of a future splitting scale on an already prescribed band width. Summable estimates for completed generations and fixed cylinders retain positive mass on a null Cantor set and exclude atoms in the limit. Uniform analytic estimates near the permanent intervals establish reflectionlessness and exclude endpoint singularities. A separate Green function estimate for thin pairs of intervals gives the Widom condition and regularity of the limiting compact set. The resulting probability measure has both a nonzero absolutely continuous component and a nonzero singular continuous component.
tldr: The paper implements the Nazarov-Volberg-Yuditskii mass-splitting construction to produce reflectionless measures with singular continuous components on Widom sets.
motivation: Reflectionless measures are central objects in spectral theory and orthogonal polynomials, and constructing examples with both absolutely continuous and singular continuous components on Widom sets is a delicate measure-theoretic problem.
method: The construction uses finite approximants with isolated atoms, replacing active atoms by permanent intervals and child atoms, with uniform analytic estimates and a Green function estimate to establish reflectionlessness and the Widom condition.
result: The resulting probability measure has nonzero absolutely continuous and singular continuous components supported on a null Cantor set, with no atoms in the limit and no endpoint singularities.
conclusion: The work provides a detailed mass-splitting scheme for reflectionless measures with singular continuous parts, advancing the theory of Widom sets and regular compact sets.

title: SOT-large Subspaces Of Non-cyclic Operators
authors: N. G. Albuquerque, G. Ara\'ujo, L. Bernal-Gonz\'alez, E. Dem\'etrio Jr., J. Seoane-Sep\'ulveda
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we consider the strong operator topology (SOT) on the space [MATH] of continuous linear operators on an infinite-dimensional Fr\'echet space [MATH]. The existence of SOT-dense subspaces as well as of SOT-closed infinite-dimensional subspaces inside the family of all non-cyclic operators is established. Other classes of operators, such as non-dense range or non-injective operators, are also studied in this regard. Moreover, we prove for the sequence space [MATH] [MATH] that the family of all non-cyclic members of [MATH] contains an isometric copy of [MATH].
tldr: This paper studies the existence of strong operator topology (SOT) dense and closed infinite-dimensional subspaces within the family of non-cyclic operators on infinite-dimensional Fréchet spaces, and shows that the non-cyclic operators on a sequence space contain an isometric copy of a certain space.
motivation: The authors aim to extend lineability and spaceability results — the study of large algebraic structures inside sets of 'pathological' or non-generic objects — from the norm topology to the strong operator topology for non-cyclic operators.
method: Using techniques from functional analysis and linear dynamics on Fréchet spaces, the authors construct explicit subspaces of non-cyclic operators that are dense or closed in the SOT, and analyze related classes such as non-dense-range and non-injective operators, also invoking isometric embedding arguments for sequence spaces.
result: They establish the existence of SOT-dense subspaces and SOT-closed infinite-dimensional subspaces consisting entirely of non-cyclic operators, prove analogous results for non-dense-range and non-injective operators, and show that the non-cyclic operators on the sequence space contain an isometric copy of a corresponding space.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that non-cyclic operators on infinite-dimensional Fréchet spaces exhibit rich algebraic and topological structure under the strong operator topology, contributing to the theory of lineability and spaceability in operator theory.

title: Data-Assimilation-Assisted Reinforcement Learning For Power Grid Control Under Load Uncertainty
authors: Ruoyu Hu, Feng Bao, Zezhong Zhang, Yanzhao Cao, Guannan Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27229v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable power grid control requires sequential decisions under transmission constraints, time-varying demand, renewable variability, and imperfect load information. We investigate how load information quality affects control in a customized transmission network simulator inspired by Grid2Op and based on a DC power flow model. The environment includes stochastic spatial loads, temporally correlated renewable-like generation, energy storage, line protection, generator dispatch, and line reconnection. An Ensemble Score Filter (EnSF) corrects noisy load information before it is passed to the controller. A heuristic study first isolates the effect of this correction under a fixed feedback rule. Proximal policy optimization (PPO) agents are then trained for sequential generator and reconnection control, frozen, and evaluated with Forward, EnSF-corrected, and Truth load information on paired stochastic scenarios. EnSF consistently lowers load estimation error. Under heuristic control, the correction extends survival and reduces warning and overload exposure. With frozen PPO policies, it increases cumulative return and keeps performance closer to the Truth benchmark, with a larger advantage when load uncertainty is amplified beyond the nominal training distribution. In both experiments, EnSF reduces load-estimation error and improves the resulting control performance in the simplified transmission network.
tldr: This paper combines data assimilation and reinforcement learning to improve power grid control under uncertain load conditions.
motivation: Reliable power grid operation requires robust sequential control despite noisy load information, renewable variability, and transmission constraints.
method: The authors use an Ensemble Score Filter to correct noisy load estimates within a Grid2Op-inspired DC power flow simulator, then train PPO agents for generator dispatch and line reconnection.
result: EnSF reduces load estimation error and improves heuristic and PPO control performance, especially when load uncertainty exceeds the nominal training distribution.
conclusion: Data-assimilation-assisted RL offers a practical way to enhance power grid control under imperfect load information in simplified transmission networks.

title: A Note On Bistability Of A Two-gene Competitive System
authors: Eduardo D. Sontag
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Positive autoregulation together with mutual competition is one of the simplest mechanisms that can produce bistability in gene-regulatory models. We study a two-gene system in which each gene activates its own expression and the two genes compete through regulatory terms with Hill exponent one. We show first that the system has at least one and at most three equilibria in the positive quadrant. Exactly two positive equilibria can occur only at a degenerate nullcline tangency; thus, in the nondegenerate case, the number of positive equilibria is one or three. If there are exactly three distinct positive equilibria, then no nondegeneracy assumption is needed: all three equilibria are automatically hyperbolic, the two outer equilibria are asymptotically stable nodes, and the middle equilibrium is a saddle. Moreover, every positive solution converges to an equilibrium. Consequently, the positive quadrant is the disjoint union of the basins of attraction of the two stable nodes and the one-dimensional stable manifold of the saddle, yielding global bistability.
tldr: A mathematical analysis of a two-gene positive autoregulation mutual competition model showing one or three positive equilibria and global bistability.
motivation: Bistability in gene regulatory networks is a fundamental phenomenon, and simple mechanisms such as positive autoregulation combined with mutual competition can produce it.
method: The paper studies a two-gene ODE system with Hill exponent one, classifies equilibria, and uses dynamical systems techniques to prove hyperbolicity and stability properties.
result: The system has at least one and at most three positive equilibria; in nondegenerate cases, the number is one or three, and when three exist, the outer two are asymptotically stable nodes while the middle is a saddle, with every positive solution converging to an equilibrium.
conclusion: The positive quadrant is partitioned into the basins of attraction of the two stable nodes and the one-dimensional stable manifold of the saddle, establishing global bistability.

title: A Strict Amplitude Lower Bound For The Van Der Pol Equation And Extensions To Symmetric Li\'enard Systems
authors: Ziwei Zhuang Changjian Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27305v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the amplitude of the unique limit cycle of the van der Pol equation [MATH] is strictly greater than [MATH] for every [MATH]. The proof combines orbit comparison in the relaxation oscillation regime, trigonometric comparison curves in the weakly nonlinear regime, and polynomial energy estimates in the intermediate regime. The polynomial sign conditions arising in the latter two regimes are certified using exact rational arithmetic and Bernstein coefficients. The orbit comparison method also applies to a class of symmetric Li\'enard systems. Under suitable monotonicity assumptions, we establish a sufficient criterion for the limit cycle amplitude to exceed a critical value determined by the damping function.
tldr: The paper proves a strict lower bound on the limit cycle amplitude of the van der Pol equation and extends the method to symmetric Liénard systems.
motivation: The van der Pol equation is a classic nonlinear oscillator, and sharp amplitude bounds are of interest in dynamical systems theory.
method: The proof combines orbit comparison in the relaxation oscillation regime, trigonometric comparison curves in the weakly nonlinear regime, and polynomial energy estimates, with polynomial sign conditions certified via exact rational arithmetic and Bernstein coefficients.
result: The unique limit cycle of the van der Pol equation is shown to have amplitude strictly greater than a specified value for every parameter, and a sufficient criterion is established for symmetric Liénard systems to exceed a critical amplitude.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous mathematical bounds for limit cycle amplitudes using a hybrid analytical and certified computational approach, with extensions beyond the van der Pol equation.

title: Entropy And Complexity In A Strong Orbit Equivalence Class Via pseudo-Toeplitz Subshifts
authors: Sebasti\'an Donoso Paulina Cecchi-Bernales
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a method for constructing minimal subshifts with a prescribed bound on the factor complexity within any strong orbit equivalence (SOE) class. This implies realizations of topological entropies within any SOE class, strengthening a series of classical results by Sugisaki. While prior work established complexity controls for zero-entropy systems, the approach of the present work extends to positive-entropy regimes. Our construction introduces the class of pseudo-Toeplitz subshifts, and we show that they exist in any SOE class. More precisely, for any [MATH] and sequence [MATH] growing exponentially at rate [MATH], we construct a system in this class whose topological entropy is [MATH] and whose complexity grows strictly faster, or, under certain conditions, slower than [MATH]. As a consequence, any Choquet simplex can be realized as the set of invariant measures of a Toeplitz subshift with precisely controlled complexity, in either a zero or positive-entropy regime.
tldr: The paper constructs pseudo-Toeplitz subshifts within any strong orbit equivalence class to realize prescribed topological entropy and control factor complexity.
motivation: Prior work controlled complexity for zero-entropy systems, but extending such constructions to positive-entropy regimes and arbitrary strong orbit equivalence classes remained open.
method: The authors introduce pseudo-Toeplitz subshifts and use them to build minimal subshifts with prescribed complexity and entropy bounds within any given strong orbit equivalence class.
result: They realize any topological entropy value in any strong orbit equivalence class and show complexity can grow strictly faster or slower than a given exponential rate under conditions; any Choquet simplex can be the invariant measure set of a controlled-complexity Toeplitz subshift.
conclusion: The work strengthens classical results of Sugisaki and provides a flexible framework for constructing symbolic dynamical systems with prescribed entropy and complexity properties.

title: Spectral-NFP: Certified Low-Rank Curvature Majorization For Accelerating Wmmse
authors: Jianhang Zhu, Tsung-Hui Chang, Kaiming Shen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27369v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weighted sum-rate maximization in multicell multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) networks is commonly addressed by the weighted minimum mean-square error (WMMSE) algorithm or fractional programming (FP), both of which, after fixing their auxiliary variables, solve a power-constrained quadratic transmit problem that requires costly dense operations for large arrays. Replacing the underlying curvature matrix with a scaled identity can avoid the matrix inverse operation and thereby reduce complexity, but it discards the curvature eigenvalue structure and yields a loose lower bound. We propose Spectral-NFP, which retains selected dominant curvature eigenpairs and uses a scaled identity matrix to bound the curvature on the remaining subspace from above. The retained rank thus traces a continuous path from NFP to the exact WMMSE transmit update. With the surrogate curvature fixed, Spectral-NFP can be interpreted as Euclidean projected-gradient ascent after a linear coordinate transformation, admitting Nesterov-type acceleration. We derive a lower bound on the one-step transmit-objective gain of Spectral-NFP relative to WMMSE, expressed in terms of the curvature eigenvalues. Under an idealized Wishart model, we analyze this bound in both finite dimensions and the large-system limit, obtaining an asymptotic rank-selection rule. Experimental results show that retaining at most 20% of the transmit dimension, and often less than 10%, achieves more than 99% of the WMMSE WSR. In large-array settings, the measured update time is below 20% of that required by WMMSE.
tldr: Spectral-NFP accelerates WMMSE for weighted sum-rate maximization in multicell MIMO networks by retaining dominant curvature eigenpairs and bounding the remainder with a scaled identity.
motivation: WMMSE and fractional programming require costly dense matrix operations for large arrays, and replacing the curvature matrix with a scaled identity discards eigenvalue structure and yields loose bounds.
method: The proposed method keeps selected dominant curvature eigenpairs, upper-bounds the remaining subspace by a scaled identity, and interprets the resulting surrogate as Euclidean projected-gradient ascent after a linear coordinate transformation, enabling Nesterov-type acceleration.
result: Retaining at most 20% and often less than 10% of the transmit dimension achieves over 99% of the WMMSE weighted sum-rate, with measured update times below 20% of WMMSE in large-array settings; an asymptotic rank-selection rule is derived under an idealized Wishart model.
conclusion: Spectral-NFP provides a certified low-rank curvature majorization framework that trades a controllable amount of optimality for substantial computational savings in MIMO beamforming optimization.

title: Linear Convergence Rate Analysis Of Proximal-Tracking For Nonsmooth Distributed Optimization
authors: Xiantao Xiao Tianyu Yuan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proximal-Tracking is a novel algorithm proposed in [Falsone and Prandini, Automatica, 135 (2022), 109938] for nonsmooth distributed consensus optimization with local set constraints. The global convergence and numerical behavior of Proximal-Tracking have been well studied in [Falsone and Prandini, Automatica, 135 (2022), 109938]. As a complement, in this paper we provide a theoretical analysis regarding its linear convergence rate under additional strong convexity and calmness assumptions. In particular, this analysis does not require assumptions such as differentiability or smoothness, thus preserving the original advantages of the algorithm.
tldr: This paper provides a theoretical analysis of the linear convergence rate of the Proximal-Tracking algorithm for nonsmooth distributed consensus optimization with local set constraints.
motivation: The Proximal-Tracking algorithm was previously studied for global convergence and numerical behavior, but its linear convergence rate under strong convexity and calmness assumptions had not been fully analyzed.
method: The authors perform a theoretical analysis using strong convexity and calmness assumptions, avoiding differentiability or smoothness requirements to preserve the algorithm's original advantages.
result: They establish a linear convergence rate for Proximal-Tracking under the additional assumptions, complementing existing convergence results.
conclusion: The work advances the theoretical understanding of a distributed optimization algorithm, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Iterates Of Ritt Operators Close To The Identity
authors: Catalin Badea
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27458v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study bounded operators whose prescribed powers remain uniformly close to the identity, and resolvent conditions sampled along sequences of powers. The displacement bound [MATH] forces a finite peripheral spectrum consisting of odd-order roots of unity and makes an explicitly determined odd power of [MATH] a Ritt operator. The sharp unconditional threshold for [MATH] itself is [MATH]. If [MATH] denotes the optimal universal Ritt resolvent bound below this threshold, then [MATH] as [MATH]. At every higher peripheral threshold the optimal finite-peripheral resolvent bound has reciprocal order of growth. We also obtain constructive bounds for general weighted Wiener symbols. For each [MATH], an angular escape invariant characterises exactly the sampling sequences for which a displacement bound by [MATH], together with the peripheral spectral condition, forces the Ritt property. We compute this invariant for asymptotically geometric sequences. At the endpoint [MATH], suitable phase conditions imply the full displacement bound without assuming power boundedness; normal contractions admit an exact scalar criterion. Finally, we establish quantitative Hilbert-space and [MATH] resolvent estimates, a characterisation of operators with odd Ritt powers on uniformly convex spaces, and strict norm gaps for operator-valued disc-algebra functions, with explicit matrix-polynomial bounds from Fej\'er--Riesz factorisation.
tldr: This paper studies bounded operators whose powers stay uniformly close to the identity, deriving peripheral spectrum constraints and connecting such operators to Ritt operators via resolvent conditions and displacement bounds.
motivation: The work is motivated by understanding when power-bounded or nearly power-bounded operators inherit Ritt-type resolvent behavior, especially under sampled resolvent conditions along sequences of powers.
method: The author uses Banach-space operator theory, resolvent estimates, peripheral spectral analysis, weighted Wiener symbols, and angular escape invariants to characterize when displacement bounds force the Ritt property.
result: The main results establish sharp thresholds for displacement bounds, finiteness and structure of the peripheral spectrum consisting of odd-order roots of unity, growth rates for optimal resolvent bounds, and constructive bounds for general weighted Wiener symbols.
conclusion: The paper provides a detailed operator-theoretic classification of iterates close to the identity, with quantitative Hilbert-space and Lp resolvent estimates and matrix-polynomial bounds from Fejer-Riesz factorization, but it is unrelated to quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: FedCoT-VQA: A Federated Learning And Unlearning Framework For Chain-of-Thought Planners In VideoQA
authors: Rui Lu, Tao Ling, Dan Wang, Qing Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) planners have emerged as an effective design for VideoQA, where a lightweight planner first generates intermediate reasoning steps to guide temporal evidence selection before answer prediction. This modularity makes CoT-based VideoQA attractive for federated learning, since only the planner side needs collaborative adaptation while the heavy vision-language backbone can remain fixed. However, in decentralized settings, the planner must not only be trained efficiently across heterogeneous clients but also support later client deletion requests. This is challenging because deleted-client influence is reflected both in model parameters and the planner's reasoning-trace behavior. We present FedCoT-VQA, a federated learning and unlearning framework for CoT planners in VideoQA. FedCoT-VQA consists of three modules: planner-side partitioning (PSP), which exposes a compact shared-residual adaptation space for efficient federated training; server-side aggregation (SSA), which aggregates planner-side updates while maintaining a deletion-ready contribution log; and a residual unlearning module (RUM), which approximates the retained-only counterfactual planner through retained-client replay and selective residual correction, without full retraining. We evaluate FedCoT-VQA in terms of federated training utility, federated unlearning utility, forgetting quality, and efficiency. Results show that compared to current federated approaches, FedCoT-VQA preserves strong federated training utility, improving grounding quality by up to 4.45%. After unlearning, it retains high accuracy and achieves a counterfactual gap of only 7.38%.
tldr: FedCoT-VQA is a federated learning and unlearning framework for chain-of-thought planners in video question answering, focused on decentralized training and client deletion without full retraining.
motivation: Federated VideoQA with CoT planners needs efficient collaborative adaptation and support for client deletion requests, where deleted-client influence appears in both parameters and reasoning traces.
method: The framework uses planner-side partitioning for compact shared-residual adaptation, server-side aggregation with a deletion-ready contribution log, and a residual unlearning module based on retained-client replay and selective residual correction.
result: It preserves federated training utility with up to 4.45% grounding improvement and after unlearning achieves high accuracy with a counterfactual gap of only 7.38%.
conclusion: FedCoT-VQA provides an effective federated learning and unlearning solution for CoT-based VideoQA, though it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Ajar: Measuring Open Privilege In Agent Defenses
authors: Reshabh K Sharma, Linxi Jiang, Shuo Chen, Zhiqiang Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26900v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A language model agent acts through the tools it is given. The data it reads while working on a task can redirect what it does with those tools. A growing set of techniques for safe and secure agent execution therefore sits between the agent and its tools, aiming to enforce access control, information flow or isolation at that boundary. Today these techniques are evaluated on agent-security benchmarks built around indirect prompt injection. Those benchmarks judge a defense by how far it brings the number of successful attacks down while preserving the agent's utility. A defense is judged only on the agent's execution. It can score well on both metrics while holding open a transfer, a deletion or a broad read that no task needed. Ajar measures that open privilege directly using the existing benchmarks. It attaches to an agent-security benchmark that already exists and reuses the tasks, tool schemas, reference solutions and goal states that benchmark uses to grade its own runs. For each benign task it builds candidate tool calls the task does not need, so allowing one is privilege left open. These calls are presented to the defense at every point where the agent could act. We evaluate Ajar by attaching it to AgentDojo, where open privilege becomes a third axis beside the existing attack success and benign utility. We run it on five defenses: Progent, CaMeL, AC4A, Permission Assistant, and Claude Code's Auto mode. We observed that they leave widely different amounts of privilege open. Two defenses leak by almost the same amount yet differ widely in the benign tasks they finish, and one defense buys part of its tightness by refusing calls its tasks were entitled to make. This open privilege cannot be derived from the measured attack success or benign utility. The source code of Ajar is available at [URL].
tldr: Ajar is a benchmark extension that measures open privilege in LLM agent defenses by testing unnecessary tool calls against existing agent-security benchmarks.
motivation: Current agent-security defenses are evaluated only on attack success and benign utility, which can hide privilege left open by a defense, such as unnecessary transfers, deletions, or broad reads.
method: Ajar attaches to AgentDojo, reuses its tasks and tool schemas, and for each benign task constructs candidate tool calls that are not needed, presenting them to the defense at every possible action point to measure open privilege as a third axis.
result: Evaluated on five defenses (Progent, CaMeL, AC4A, Permission Assistant, and Claude Code's Auto mode), Ajar found widely different amounts of open privilege, including defenses with similar leakage but different benign task completion and one defense that improves tightness by refusing entitled calls.
conclusion: Open privilege is a distinct and previously unmeasured property of agent defenses that cannot be inferred from attack success or benign utility, motivating its use as an additional evaluation axis.

title: Improving Service Availability In KubeEdge-Based Architectures Using Lightweight Intrusion Detection
authors: Harrol Ndjeudji Kuibou, Mostafa Anouar Ghorab, Mohamed Aymen Saied
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27052v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The increasing adoption of the Internet of Things (IoT) and cloud computing has accelerated the evolution of edge computing paradigms [1]. Industry forecasts estimate that the number of connected IoT devices will reach approximately 50 billion by 2030, following an estimated 38 billion connections by 2025 [34], resulting in an unprecedented growth in data generation. This trend necessitates efficient, scalable, and secure data processing mechanisms at the network edge. Consequently, ensuring the reliable management and protection of IoT applications and devices has become a critical challenge. In this context, KubeEdge extends cloud-native capabilities to edge environments, enabling distributed orchestration while introducing new security concerns. This paper investigates the security of container images in IoT-driven and distributed edge architectures. Specifically, we analyze the impact of major security threats, including Denial of Service (DoS) attacks and malicious container deployments, on the availability and operational stability of KubeEdge-based systems. To address these challenges, we propose a lightweight Recommended Intrusion Detection Rule Set (RIDRS) tailored for resource-constrained edge environments. The proposed approach improves system resilience by enabling timely detection and mitigation of security threats. We define system stability as the ability to maintain consistent operational behavior and to recover autonomously under adversarial conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that RIDRS significantly reduces system downtime and enhances service availability, particularly in scenarios involving code injection and malicious pod deployment attacks.
tldr: This paper proposes a lightweight intrusion detection rule set (RIDRS) to improve service availability and resilience in KubeEdge-based IoT edge architectures against DoS and malicious container deployment attacks.
motivation: The rapid growth of IoT and edge computing, particularly with KubeEdge, introduces new security threats that can degrade service availability in resource-constrained environments.
method: The authors analyze security threats to container images in KubeEdge-based systems and develop a lightweight Recommended Intrusion Detection Rule Set (RIDRS) tailored for edge environments.
result: Experimental evaluation shows that RIDRS reduces system downtime and enhances service availability under code injection and malicious pod deployment attacks.
conclusion: Lightweight intrusion detection can effectively improve the operational stability and security of KubeEdge-based IoT edge deployments.

title: Cryptographic Security Is Not Enough: Privacy Gaps In The Renegade Decentralized Dark Pool
authors: Prerna Arote, Adrian Saiz, Oriol Saguillo, Lucianna Kiffer
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dark pools are designed to provide pre-trade privacy, liveness, and post-trade confidentiality - concealing order flow before execution and limiting information leakage after. Decentralized dark pools, such as Renegade, aim to replicate these properties without custodial risk, using secure multi-party computation (MPC) and zero-knowledge proofs for private order matching and verifiable settlement. We show that Renegade's cryptographic guarantees do not deliver these dark pool properties in practice. MPC-with-abort ensures correctness but not fairness: a party may learn the match result and abort without penalty, breaking pre-trade privacy. We demonstrate that the protocol's discovery layer further leaks trading intent before MPC even begins, and that sustained probing via selective abort can probabilistically reconstruct counterparty order history, threatening post-trade confidentiality. We also show that the absence of input-consistency checks prior to MPC execution enables a griefing attack using invalid state commitments requiring no real token holdings that continuously locks honest users' wallets and wastes compute, breaking liveness under sustained conditions. We further analyze over 700,000 Renegade transactions on Base and probe the P2P layer, finding that the network is effectively centralized: 88% of traffic routes through a handful of relayers, with only four nodes sustaining the P2P layer. Since relayers hold their users' wallet state in plaintext, this concentration means the system operates as a centralized orderbook in practice - reproducing off-chain the information asymmetry that dark pools are designed to eliminate. Together, our results show that cryptographic privacy does not imply dark pool security: pre-trade privacy, liveness, and post-trade confidentiality each require additional protocol-level guarantees beyond MPC correctness.
tldr: The paper shows that Renegade's cryptographic MPC and zero-knowledge guarantees fail to provide dark pool privacy, liveness, and confidentiality in practice.
motivation: Decentralized dark pools aim to offer pre-trade privacy, liveness, and post-trade confidentiality without custodial risk, but it is unclear whether cryptographic correctness alone suffices.
method: The authors analyze the Renegade protocol, demonstrate attacks exploiting MPC-with-abort, discovery-layer leakage, lack of input-consistency checks, and probe its P2P network and on-chain transactions.
result: They find that selective abort can reconstruct order history, invalid state commitments enable griefing attacks, and 88% of traffic routes through a few relayers, making the network effectively centralized.
conclusion: Cryptographic privacy does not imply dark pool security; additional protocol-level guarantees beyond MPC correctness are needed for pre-trade privacy, liveness, and post-trade confidentiality.

title: Agentic-IC3: Enabling Semantic Proof Search In Ic3 Model Checking
authors: Yu-Wei Fan, Soohyuk Cho, Aarti Gupta, Sharad Malik
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: IC3 is a state-of-the-art algorithm for hardware model checking that proves safety properties by incrementally constructing an inductive invariant consisting of a set of lemmas. Its effectiveness depends on generalization heuristics that identify useful lemmas and guide proof search. However, many leading IC3 hardware model checkers operate on lowered, bit-level representations, where high-level design relationships are difficult to exploit for generalization. Those operating at a higher level remain limited in exploiting high-level design structure and semantics. We present Agentic-IC3, built on Pono's word-level model-checking infrastructure, which integrates a language-model agent into IC3 to guide semantic proof search using register-transfer-level (RTL) design information. The framework exposes an agent-oriented interface to a persistent IC3 backend, allowing the agent to interact with an explicit, evolving proof state throughout verification. Across successive proof obligations, the agent relates intermediate proof states and solver feedback to the RTL and proposes high-level lemmas through both SAT and UNSAT generalization. Beyond generalization, the agent can introduce derived observation signals to express design relationships succinctly and obtain more informative feedback, and backtrack to revise proposals that lead to unproductive proof branches. The backend checks proposals before updating the proof state, preserving soundness and providing feedback for further reasoning. On a suite of 14 benchmarks spanning security information-flow verification and functional verification of communication protocols, processors, and functional units, Agentic-IC3 solves 10 cases within a one-hour timeout, including 4 unsolved by all three evaluated baselines: rIC3, Pono-IC3Bits, and A-IC3.
tldr: Agentic-IC3 integrates a language-model agent into the IC3 hardware model-checking algorithm to guide semantic proof search using RTL design information.
motivation: IC3 model checkers often operate on bit-level representations and struggle to exploit high-level design structure for lemma generalization and proof search.
method: The framework exposes an agent-oriented interface to a persistent IC3 backend, allowing the agent to relate proof states and solver feedback to RTL, propose high-level lemmas via SAT/UNSAT generalization, introduce derived observation signals, and backtrack on unproductive branches.
result: On 14 benchmarks covering security information-flow and functional verification, Agentic-IC3 solves 10 cases within a one-hour timeout, including 4 cases unsolved by rIC3, Pono-IC3Bits, and A-IC3 baselines.
conclusion: Language-model-guided semantic proof search can improve IC3 hardware verification by exploiting RTL-level information while preserving soundness through backend checks.

title: Pacing Equilibria In Abstract Mechanisms
authors: Christian Kroer Salam Afiouni
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27285v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital platforms increasingly rely on automated budget-management systems to regulate participation across allocation opportunities. A common tool is multiplicative pacing, which scales buyers' bids so that campaign-level budgets are spent gradually. Although pacing is operationally simple, its aggregate behavior depends on the underlying mechanism. In first-price single-item auction markets, pacing enjoys strong structural and computational properties that often fail in second-price auctions. It is unclear whether these properties extend to richer platform mechanisms. We develop a unified theory of pacing equilibria across a hierarchy of mechanisms. We first show that, even in first-price position auctions, the market-equilibrium interpretation of the single-item benchmark can fail. We then identify bid-maximizing pay-your-bid mechanisms as a broad class in which pacing equilibria exist, are unique, and admit an Eisenberg-Gale-type convex-program characterization. This implies efficient computation, Pareto-efficiency, and liquid-welfare guarantees, enabling pacing integration into large-scale optimization-based allocation routines. Finally, for abstract mechanisms satisfying a payment monotonicity condition, we prove equilibrium existence by smoothing discontinuities. With additional conditions and appropriate tie-breaking, we obtain uniqueness, revenue maximality among budget-feasible pacing vectors, and shill-proof implementability, and provide convergent budget-adjustment dynamics for approximate equilibria. Overall, many favorable properties of first-price pacing extend beyond single-item auctions under appropriate mechanism-level conditions.
tldr: Develops a unified theory of pacing equilibria across a hierarchy of auction mechanisms, showing existence and uniqueness for bid-maximizing pay-your-bid mechanisms and proving existence for abstract mechanisms under payment monotonicity.
motivation: Digital platforms use multiplicative pacing for budget management, but existing structural properties from first-price single-item auctions may fail in richer mechanisms, necessitating a broader theoretical understanding.
method: Theoretical analysis of pacing equilibria, including an Eisenberg-Gale-type convex program characterization for bid-maximizing pay-your-bid mechanisms and a smoothing technique for discontinuities in abstract mechanisms.
result: Pacing equilibria exist and are unique in bid-maximizing pay-your-bid mechanisms; for abstract mechanisms satisfying payment monotonicity, existence is proven, with additional conditions yielding uniqueness, revenue maximality, shill-proof implementability, and convergent budget-adjustment dynamics.
conclusion: Many favorable properties of first-price pacing extend beyond single-item auctions under appropriate mechanism-level conditions, enabling integration into large-scale optimization-based allocation routines.

title: Sagegan: Style-Based Anomaly Detection With Gaussian Embeddings Using Generative Adversarial Networks
authors: Thesath Wijayasiri, Kar Wai Fok, Vrizlynn L. L. Thing
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Malware evolves faster than rule-based and signature-driven detection pipelines. This paper presents SAGEGAN, a benign-only trained malware anomaly detection framework that converts portable executable files into compact three-channel images and models benign structure through style-conditioned adversarial reconstruction. The representation combines Hilbert-mapped byte values, benign-referenced byte-transition surprise, and entropy deviation from benign software. The model encodes each image into a layer-wise style tensor aligned with a seven-stage modulated generator, rather than a single latent bottleneck. A Gaussian style prior, moment-based prior alignment, and latent consistency are used to reduce mismatch between encoded benign styles and the generator's sampled manifold. For interpretation, a deterministic encoder pathway maps each executable to a fixed style tensor, enabling repeatable layer-wise family distance, gradient sensitivity, principal component, and class-behaviour analyses. On a self-collected portable executable corpus containing malware from 214 families, the Gaussian variant achieves 89.76% area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and 88.19% balanced accuracy, while the genome-style variant reaches 88.03% and 84.09%, respectively. Without refitting model weights, benign reference statistics, or decision thresholds, the same checkpoints are evaluated on DIKE, Microsoft BIG 2015, and Lester malware subsets. The results suggest that layer-wise style modelling supports both anomaly ranking and structured post hoc analysis of how malware families depart from the benign manifold.
tldr: SAGEGAN is a benign-only malware anomaly detection framework that encodes portable executables as three-channel images and uses style-based generative adversarial networks with Gaussian latent embeddings to detect and analyze malware families.
motivation: Malware evolves faster than rule-based and signature-driven detection methods, motivating anomaly detection trained only on benign software to identify novel malicious deviations.
method: The framework converts portable executables into three-channel images using Hilbert-mapped bytes, byte-transition surprise, and entropy deviation, then models benign structure through a seven-stage modulated generator guided by layer-wise style tensors and a Gaussian style prior.
result: On a corpus of 214 malware families, the Gaussian variant achieves 89.76% AUROC and 88.19% balanced accuracy, while the genome-style variant reaches 88.03% and 84.09%, respectively, with cross-dataset evaluation on DIKE, Microsoft BIG 2015, and Lester subsets.
conclusion: Layer-wise style modelling supports both malware anomaly ranking and structured post hoc analysis of how malware families depart from the benign manifold, suggesting a promising direction for interpretable anomaly detection.

title: Seal, Then Sample: Sampled Layerwise Proofs For Verifiable Llm Inference From Gpt-2 To 70b
authors: Sam Yong Youki Lim
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Verifying outsourced language-model inference requires a precisely identified computation and an audit whose cost a service can afford. We present Sampled Layerwise Proofs (SLP), a protocol and prototype that commits the boundary activations of every chunk of an inference trace, absorbs all commitments before any challenge is drawn, and then proves a verifier-selected subset of chunks together with the chunks that bind the prompt and the answer. Audit coverage becomes a runtime parameter over one set of commitments: on a TinyLlama-1.1B trace, proving seven of 47 chunks takes 22.0% of the time and 6.8% of the proof size of proving all 47. Because proof cost is dominated by weights rather than tokens, SLP packs concurrent requests into one trace under a block-diagonal causal mask and binds the prompt and answer of each request to its slot. Twelve packed requests are proved in 181.9 s, 6.5 times less than twelve separate proofs at the measured single-proof cost, and a simulated service proves twelve requests at 30.6 s per request with 0.6 s of verification each, rejecting a tampered answer. Disk-backed integer weights and streamed polynomial commitments let a single Llama-2-70B run complete on a 2 TB CPU host: 163 chunks sealed, five proved, a 4.34 MiB proof in 1,259 s, verified in 46.3 s without the weights. The proven object is a fixed-point canonical model; we trace a severe fidelity loss to the residual-stream bit width, repair it with an LLM-aware observer, and measure 84.8-84.9% argmax agreement with the floating-point reference over 334,705 WikiText-2 test positions. The limits are stated as precisely: guarantees cover proven chunks only, a fixed invalid chunk in the 70B setting is covered with probability 3/161, a manifest-only Fiat-Shamir schedule can be ground at 12.5 ms per attempt and needs an externally ordered challenge, and all measurements use a test reference string.
tldr: SLP is a cryptographic protocol for verifiable outsourced LLM inference that commits to layerwise activation chunks and proves a runtime-selected subset.
motivation: Verifying outsourced language-model inference requires a precisely identified computation and an affordable audit mechanism.
method: The protocol seals boundary activations of every inference chunk, absorbs all commitments before challenge, then proves verifier-selected chunks plus prompt/answer-binding chunks using streamed polynomial commitments and a block-diagonal causal mask for packed requests.
result: On TinyLlama-1.1B, proving 7 of 47 chunks takes 22.0% of time and 6.8% of proof size versus proving all; a Llama-2-70B run seals 163 chunks with five proved and a 4.34 MiB proof verified in 46.3 s, with 84.8-84.9% argmax agreement.
conclusion: SLP enables tunable audit coverage for LLM inference but only guarantees proven chunks, and the Fiat-Shamir schedule has limitations; it does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Extracting CNNs In The Unknown-Architecture And Feedback-Agnostic Setting
authors: Jiashuo Liu, Ruijie Ma, Manman Li, Yi Chen, Shaozhen Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27427v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies the cryptanalytic extraction of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Existing cryptanalytic extraction attacks on CNNs assume that the network architecture is known, and try to recover model parameters.In this paper, we prove for the first time that the architecture assumption can be removed for CNNs with both max and average pooling. Our core finding is that the spatial geometry of the weight vectors recovered by existing parameter-recovery attacks naturally leaks the architecture. We formalize this geometry and establish its correspondence with the architectural knowledge of a convolutional layer: (1) The sparsity consistency with the convolution receptive field reveals the layer type, the kernel size, and the stride; (2) The numerical consistency with the kernel parameters reveals the padding mode and the output-channel number; (3) The structural consistency with the pooling operation reveals the pooling type, the window size, and the stride. Although the recovered vectors are obtained using different methods in the raw-output and hard label settings, their spatial geometry remains the same. Therefore, our architecture recovery is feedback-agnostic: combined with a parameter-recovery attack, it yields a complete cryptanalytic extraction framework that recovers both the architecture and the parameters in the black-box setting. Extensive experiments, including both layer-wise and end-to-end ones, on a wide range of CNNs demonstrate that simultaneously recovering the network architecture and the model parameters is practical.
tldr: The paper introduces a cryptanalytic extraction framework that recovers both the architecture and parameters of CNNs in a black-box, feedback-agnostic setting by exploiting the spatial geometry of recovered weight vectors.
motivation: Existing cryptanalytic extraction attacks on CNNs assume the network architecture is known, which limits their applicability in realistic black-box scenarios.
method: The authors formalize the spatial geometry of weight vectors recovered by parameter-recovery attacks, showing that sparsity, numerical, and structural consistencies reveal layer type, kernel size, stride, padding mode, output-channel number, and pooling details.
result: Extensive layer-wise and end-to-end experiments on a wide range of CNNs demonstrate that simultaneously recovering architecture and parameters is practical in both raw-output and hard-label settings.
conclusion: The architecture assumption can be removed for CNNs with max and average pooling, yielding a complete feedback-agnostic cryptanalytic extraction framework.

title: Control-Token Injection Suppresses Chain-of-Thought And Defeats Reasoning-Based Oversight In Tool-Using Agents
authors: Muhammad Usama, Khair Un Nisa, Summer Yeoreum Jung
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The safety of a tool-using language model agent is usually treated as a property of the model alone. We give controlled, full-precision evidence that it is instead a joint property of the model and the software that renders its chat template and parses its tool calls, the decoding harness, and that both halves are attackable from untrusted input. On the released gpt-oss-20b reasoning model under its published tool sandbox, appending a single string of the model's own channel-control tokens to a user message makes the tokenizer render a reasoning turn that is already complete, so the model writes no chain-of-thought and proceeds directly to the tool call. Across forty tasks the model already completes, the reasoning channel falls from a mean of 52.5 tokens to zero on every trial while the http.post still fires on every trial. A rule monitor and a cross-family language-model monitor detect the unsafe request on all plain trials and no forged trials, and on overtly malicious requests the attack converts 39.6% of the model's refusals into completed exfiltrations. Separately, whether an identical tool-call generation fires is decided by the harness parser, not the model: a truncation-tolerant regular expression fires a call whose closing token is missing while a strict one drops it, and two parsers shipped for the Gemma agent give opposite outcomes on identical greedy generations, firing on all twenty-four trials and on none. We show the suppression can be delivered indirectly and characterize its dependence on the chat template across two more reasoning models, and we evaluate input sanitization, parser hardening, and empty-reasoning detection as defenses; flagging an absent trace catches the basic attack but not an adaptive benign decoy. All measurements use greedy decoding on publicly released models. Code and per-trial logs: [URL].
tldr: The paper demonstrates that appending control tokens to user input suppresses chain-of-thought reasoning in tool-using LLM agents and can bypass reasoning-based safety monitors, while harness parsers also determine whether tool calls execute.
motivation: Safety of tool-using language model agents is often treated as a model-only property, but the authors argue it is jointly determined by the model, chat template, decoding harness, and tool-call parser.
method: Using controlled full-precision experiments with greedy decoding on gpt-oss-20b, Gemma, and other reasoning models, they inject channel-control tokens into user messages, vary parsers, and test monitors plus defenses such as input sanitization, parser hardening, and empty-reasoning detection.
result: The attack reduces mean reasoning tokens from 52.5 to zero across forty tasks while unsafe HTTP POST calls still fire, converts 39.6% of refusals into completed exfiltrations, and shows that strict versus truncation-tolerant parsers give opposite outcomes on identical generations.
conclusion: Agent safety must account for the whole software stack, and basic defenses such as flagging absent reasoning traces catch the simple attack but fail against an adaptive benign decoy.

title: Cost Sharing With Hidden Time Flexibility
authors: Farzaneh Rajabighamchi Mohsen Pourpouneh
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Customers often specify acceptable time intervals for receiving a service. When service on a date entails a fixed activation cost, overlapping intervals allow joint service and cost sharing. Customers may nevertheless conceal flexibility by reporting a smaller interval, affecting both operating cost and its allocation. We ask whether an operator can select a core allocation at every reported profile without making concealment profitable. We establish sharp population boundaries for preventing such coalitional reductions. When intervals may be narrowed from either end, a core-selecting rule preventing such reductions exists if and only if there are at most three customers. With four or more customers, impossibility holds even under Pareto contraction-proofness, which excludes deviations making every contracting customer weakly better off and at least one strictly better off. The impossibility persists when each contracting customer conceals only an arbitrarily small fraction of her feasible interval. The boundaries change when either the earliest or latest acceptable date of every customer is verifiable. With common verified dates, equal sharing is core-selecting and prevents such reductions for any population size. When verified dates may differ, the boundary rises to five: such a rule exists for up to five customers, whereas with six or more no core-selecting rule prevents the contracting customers from reducing their combined payment. Under Pareto contraction-proofness, however, core selection is possible for every population size on either one-sided domain. Finally, the relaxations needed for approximate core selection and coalitional contraction-proofness must grow with population size.
tldr: The paper studies cost-sharing mechanisms where customers may strategically conceal time flexibility, deriving sharp population boundaries for core-selecting rules that prevent profitable coalitional reductions.
motivation: Customers with overlapping acceptable service intervals can share activation costs, but they may underreport their flexibility to manipulate both operating costs and allocations.
method: The authors analyze core-selecting cost-sharing rules on reported interval profiles, using cooperative game theory and mechanism design to characterize when concealment can be prevented under one-sided or two-sided interval narrowing and verifiability assumptions.
result: With two-sided interval narrowing, prevention is possible iff there are at most three customers; with four or more, impossibility holds even under Pareto contraction-proofness. Verifiable common dates allow equal sharing for any population, while differing verified dates raise the boundary to five, and approximate core selection requires relaxations growing with population size.
conclusion: Hidden time flexibility imposes severe limits on core-selecting cost-sharing mechanisms, and only strong verifiability or approximate solutions can overcome the impossibility results.

title: Agent-based Modeling: Equilibrium, Echo Chambers, And Efficiency In Hybrid Coevolutionary Opinion Games
authors: Ming-Zhi Jiang, An-Tzi Teng, Jun-En Liu, Po-An Chen, Yung-Ming Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Opinion formation in online networks involves changes in both beliefs and social ties. Analytical models make it possible to study equilibrium and social cost, but usually represent communication as a fixed numerical update. LLM-driven agents offer a language-based alternative, yet their convergence and collective efficiency remain unclear. We develop the Hybrid Coevolutionary Opinion Game (H-COG), combining cost-minimizing Friedkin-Johnsen agents (Type-C) and Phi-4 language agents (Type-L) in a dynamically rewired K-nearest-neighbor network. We initialize 50 agents with opinions drawn from 5,199 Reddit comments on gun control and abortion. The comments are scored on a continuous [-1,+1] scale using a fine-tuned RoBERTa regressor, and a mixing parameter sets the proportion of each agent type. The experiments cover nine population compositions, three initial network topologies, and two topics. All 540 runs meet the convergence criterion within the simulation horizon. Under Type-L updating, the coevolving network reaches an attractor as reliably as it does under the analytical update rule, making an equilibrium-based efficiency comparison possible. The pooled Price of Anarchy is [MATH] for purely Type-L populations, compared with [MATH] for purely Type-C populations. A decomposition of social cost attributes most of this gap to language agents moving away from their intrinsic opinions, rather than to greater disagreement with their neighbors. The main findings are consistent across the three initial network topologies.
tldr: The paper introduces a hybrid coevolutionary opinion game combining analytical and LLM agents, finding that LLM agents reach equilibrium but with higher social cost.
motivation: Analytical opinion models are limited by fixed numerical updates, while LLM-driven agents offer a language-based alternative, but their convergence and collective efficiency are unclear.
method: They simulate 50 agents on a rewired KNN network, mixing Friedkin-Johnsen (Type-C) and Phi-4 language agents (Type-L), initialized with opinions from Reddit comments scored by a fine-tuned RoBERTa regressor.
result: All 540 runs converge; purely Type-L populations have a higher Price of Anarchy than purely Type-C, mainly due to language agents deviating from intrinsic opinions rather than increased disagreement.
conclusion: The findings suggest LLM agents can reliably reach an attractor but incur greater efficiency loss in opinion formation games.

title: Network-based Modeling Of Cocaine Trafficking Flows And Displacement Effects
authors: H. A. (bart), Peters, Frederike Oetker, Robby Roks, Roy Lindelauf, Robbert Fokkink, Huijuan Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26864v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The worldwide cocaine market is undergoing an extraordinary surge. Insights on how cocaine is trafficked from production countries to consumer markets are limited, and often based on observed trafficking routes (e.g., seizures) alone. In this paper, we introduce a network-based model of actual transnational cocaine flows, beyond flows seized. In this model, cocaine is routed through an international transportation network of land and sea connections, where each link is assigned an interception risk metric for containerized transport. This interception risk metric combines features related to law enforcement inspections, containerized trade, and transport connectivity into three key driving components of interception risk using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). The interception risk metric on each link is then constructed from these driving components, where the importance of each component is characterized by a strength parameter. Given a set of strength parameters, cocaine is assumed to be routed from production countries to consumption countries via routes that minimize the total risk of interception, subject to country-specific supply and demand constraints. In the end, the strength parameters are calibrated by comparing the corresponding flow outcomes with known trafficking activity. From these final trafficking flows associated with the calibrated parameters, we are able to identify `blind spots' (e.g., nonzero flows on links with small or none observed trafficking activity) and provide more evidence of the waterbed effect (e.g., changing routes as a result of increased interdiction efforts by law enforcement).
tldr: The paper builds a network-based model of transnational cocaine trafficking flows that infers unobserved routes by minimizing interception risk subject to supply and demand constraints.
motivation: Insights into global cocaine trafficking are largely limited to seized shipments, so the authors aim to estimate actual flows and the displacement ('waterbed') effects caused by interdiction efforts.
method: A PCA-derived link-level interception risk metric is constructed from law-enforcement, containerized trade, and transport connectivity features, and cocaine is routed through the land/sea transport network along minimum-risk paths subject to country supply-demand constraints, with strength parameters calibrated against known trafficking activity.
result: The calibrated model reproduces observed trafficking patterns, reveals 'blind spots' with nonzero inferred flows on links showing little or no seizure activity, and provides additional evidence for the waterbed effect under increased interdiction.
conclusion: Network-based flow modeling with calibrated risk metrics can extend beyond seizure data to characterize actual trafficking routes and anticipate displacement effects of enforcement.

title: Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal For Gradient Descent: The Strongly Convex Case
authors: Yuhan Ye Kaizhao Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.26873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study gradient descent with predetermined nonnegative stepsizes on smooth strongly convex functions. Let [MATH] and [MATH] be the condition number. We prove the iteration lower bound [MATH] for both relative squared distance and relative function error, uniformly over [MATH] and sufficiently large [MATH]. This matches the polynomial exponent of [MATH] for the Silver stepsize schedule established in [Altschuler and Parrilo, 2025].
tldr: The paper proves that the Silver stepsize schedule is (almost) optimal for gradient descent on smooth strongly convex functions by establishing a matching iteration lower bound.
motivation: The Silver stepsize schedule recently achieved improved convergence exponents for gradient descent, but it was unclear whether its polynomial rate could be improved by any predetermined nonnegative stepsize sequence.
method: The authors derive an iteration complexity lower bound for gradient descent with arbitrary predetermined nonnegative stepsizes on smooth strongly convex objectives, uniform over the condition number and sufficiently large iteration counts.
result: They prove a lower bound matching the polynomial exponent in the condition number achieved by the Silver stepsize schedule, for both relative squared distance and relative function error.
conclusion: The Silver schedule is essentially optimal within the class of predetermined stepsizes for strongly convex gradient descent, closing the gap between upper and lower bounds.

title: Stochastic Appointment Scheduling With Patient-and-Time-Dependent Probability Distributions
authors: Hossein Hashemi Doulabi Soheyl Khalilpourazari
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27016v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Outpatient appointment scheduling must balance provider idle time, overtime, and patient waiting under uncertain service times, punctuality, and attendance. These factors may follow patient-and-time-dependent probability distributions, which existing models rarely incorporate simultaneously because of modeling and computational complexity. We propose a stochastic programming model that captures exponentially many scenarios with polynomially many variables and constraints, without sampling. It accommodates patient-dependent service times and patient-and-time-dependent no-shows and arrival times. We also discuss estimating these distributions from electronic health records. We examine how personalized reminders and changes in attendance due to incentives or negative clinic experiences affect scheduling. Our model optimally solves instances of up to 14 patients in reasonable computational time. Its schedules outperform classical Bailey-type rules. Even the best-performing variant has 97% higher expected cost on average. Incorporating patient-dependent service times reduces total costs by 34% on average. Accounting for patient-and-time-dependent unpunctuality and no-shows reduces costs by 12% and 67%, respectively. Personalized reminders can reduce costs by 23%, and sensitivity analyses show that these gains withstand moderate errors in estimated distributions. These findings show how modeling individual patient behavior and tailoring communication can reduce waiting, idle time, and overtime.
tldr: This paper develops a stochastic programming model for outpatient appointment scheduling that incorporates patient-and-time-dependent distributions for service times, no-shows, and arrival punctuality.
motivation: Existing appointment scheduling models rarely simultaneously account for patient-dependent service times and time-dependent attendance and punctuality because of modeling and computational complexity.
method: The authors propose a scenario-based stochastic programming formulation with exponentially many scenarios but polynomially many variables and constraints, avoiding sampling, and discuss estimating the required distributions from electronic health records.
result: The model optimally solves instances up to 14 patients and yields schedules that outperform Bailey-type rules, with average cost reductions of 34% from patient-dependent service times, 12% from unpunctuality, 67% from no-shows, and 23% from personalized reminders.
conclusion: The findings demonstrate that modeling individual patient behavior and tailoring communication can substantially reduce waiting, idle time, and overtime in outpatient scheduling.

title: Twisted Patterson-Sullivan Densities On Nilpotent Covers For Anosov Subgroups
authors: Neelanjan Mondal Krishnendu Gongopadhyay
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27125v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a Zariski-dense Borel-Anosov subgroup and let [MATH] be positive on its limit cone. For every [MATH], we construct twisted [MATH]-conformal densities and prove their uniqueness, atomlessness, and ergodicity. For every normal subgroup [MATH] with nilpotent quotient, we classify the ergodic [MATH]-conformal densities of [MATH] in terms of characters of [MATH].
tldr: The paper constructs and classifies twisted Patterson-Sullivan conformal densities on nilpotent covers for Zariski-dense Borel-Anosov subgroups, proving uniqueness, atomlessness, and ergodicity.
motivation: Patterson-Sullivan theory connects conformal densities at infinity with the ergodic theory of discrete group actions, and the authors aim to extend this framework to twisted settings and nilpotent covers for Anosov subgroups beyond rank-one cases.
method: The authors use tools from geometric group theory and hyperbolic dynamics — limit cones, Anosov representations, conformal densities, and character theory for nilpotent quotients — to construct twisted densities and classify ergodic ones.
result: They prove existence, uniqueness, atomlessness, and ergodicity of twisted conformal densities for every character, and classify ergodic conformal densities on normal subgroups with nilpotent quotient in terms of characters.
conclusion: The work generalizes Patterson-Sullivan theory to higher-rank Anosov settings with nilpotent covers, providing a character-based classification of ergodic conformal densities.

title: Stochastic Augmented Lagrangian Framework With Second-Order Convergence Guarantees For Nonconvex Expectation-Constrained Optimization
authors: Yash Kumar Raghu Bollapragada
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we propose and analyze an augmented Lagrangian framework for solving stochastic nonconvex optimization problems with expectation-based equality constraints over a closed and convex constraint set. The framework generates a sequence of nonconvex primal subproblems, which are solved inexactly using stochastic second-order methods. We establish iteration complexity results for obtaining approximate second-order stationary points, both in expectation and with prescribed probability, under corresponding conditions on the accuracy of the primal subproblem solutions. We further establish sample complexity results for the framework with general stochastic second-order subproblem solvers under reasonable assumptions on their theoretical guarantees. Moreover, we incorporate three existing stochastic second-order solvers and derive the corresponding deterministic and probabilistic sample complexity results for obtaining approximate second-order stationary points. To the best of our knowledge, such sample complexity guarantees for obtaining approximate second-order stationary points in nonconvex expectation-constrained optimization have not been established previously. Finally, we demonstrate the empirical performance of the proposed framework on two nonconvex machine learning problems.
tldr: This paper develops a stochastic augmented Lagrangian framework for nonconvex expectation-constrained optimization with second-order convergence and sample-complexity guarantees.
motivation: Nonconvex optimization with expectation-based constraints is important for machine learning, but existing methods lack second-order stationarity and sample complexity guarantees.
method: The authors generate a sequence of nonconvex primal subproblems solved inexactly via stochastic second-order solvers, and analyze iteration and sample complexity under accuracy conditions on the subproblem solutions.
result: They derive deterministic and probabilistic iteration complexity and sample complexity bounds for obtaining approximate second-order stationary points, instantiating three existing stochastic second-order solvers.
conclusion: The framework provides the first sample complexity guarantees for second-order stationarity in nonconvex expectation-constrained optimization, demonstrated on two machine learning problems.

title: The Ball-Covering Property In Lipschitz-Free Spaces
authors: Ram\'on J. Aliaga, Colin Petitjean, Anton\'in Proch\'azka, Daniele Puglisi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27485v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study ball-covering properties in Lipschitz-free spaces. We establish an extension criterion for proving that [MATH] fails the ball-covering property and apply it to several classes of nonseparable metric spaces. In contrast, we construct a nonseparable uniformly discrete metric space [MATH] such that [MATH] has the uniform ball-covering property and is isomorphic to [MATH]. More precisely, [MATH] has the [MATH]-ball-covering property for every [MATH]. This example also shows that these quantitative ball-covering properties are not hereditary within the class of Lipschitz-free spaces. Finally, we prove some stability results under sufficiently small bi-Lipschitz perturbations of the metric.
tldr: This pure-mathematics paper studies ball-covering properties in Lipschitz-free spaces, establishing extension criteria, constructing nonseparable examples with the uniform ball-covering property, and proving stability under small bi-Lipschitz perturbations.
motivation: The authors aim to understand when Lipschitz-free spaces (a Banach-space-theoretic construction) fail or satisfy ball-covering properties, extending known results to nonseparable metric spaces.
method: They develop an extension criterion for showing failure of the ball-covering property, apply it to classes of nonseparable metric spaces, and construct a nonseparable uniformly discrete metric space yielding a Lipschitz-free space with quantitative ball-covering properties.
result: They identify broad classes of nonseparable metric spaces whose Lipschitz-free spaces lack the ball-covering property, while exhibiting a counterexample with the M-ball-covering property for every parameter, showing these properties are not hereditary, and proving stability under sufficiently small bi-Lipschitz perturbations.
conclusion: The findings advance the geometric and isomorphic theory of Lipschitz-free spaces, but have no evident connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: The Like Trap: Multi-Stage Poisoning Against Agents In Similarity-based Recommendation Systems
authors: Yue Xing, Pengfei He, Zitao Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.27155v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents, these agents are becoming increasingly autonomous and gaining broader access to act on users' behalf on the internet. However, the vulnerability of automated agents deployed on social media platforms (e.g., for managing a user's personal account) remains underexplored. Existing studies on agent poisoning typically assume that the adversary can expose poisoned content to the agent. Although such an attack is direct and effective, it is more easily detected and mitigated. In the context of social media platforms, this leaves open whether the recommendation system itself would surface such content to the agent in a more subtle manner. Through theoretical analysis, we show that the like-score mechanism used in OASIS can be exploited, and we characterize the conditions under which a multi-stage chain of poisoned posts can steer the agent's feed. Based on these insights, we further develop an algorithm that crafts realistic poisoned posts.
